It further reveals that the performance of school leavers on English literacy tests stood at an average of 50% for all literacy skills measured. Moreover, the pupils poorest performance in terms oforganisation/flow of ideas, grammar/spelling, andchoice of vocabularyliteracy skills was evident for schools in rural areas. The study concludes that many primary school leavers acquired English literacy skills that were less than the expected threshold level for the learners smooth academic progression at post-primary education in Tanzania, according to CEFR standards and Cummins (1979) theory of Cognitive Academic Language Proficiency (CALP). The implications of the findings are discussed to enhance policy and transform English literacy practices in the country.
Title: Assessing teachers pedagogical practices and adequacy of English literacy skills acquired by primary school children in Tanzania

Abstract: To create a more racially diverse campus, it is not only important for the students and the faculty to be educated, but for them to be empowered. In academia, understanding those functions attributed to Black faculty does not automatically translate into an appreciation of the deep-rooted structural and institutional culpability when it comes to matters involving racialized differentials. This means that institutional expectations are oftentimes unrealistic and based on whiteness, with no regard for the experiences of confronting racism embedded in the professional trajectories of Black tenure line professors. The objective of this study is to problematize activities of research in the academic environment from the perspective of such university professors working in Brazil and the USA. Within a collaborative qualitative self-study perspective, we have analyzed (auto)biographical narrativesusingS-STEPmethodologythat serves our agenda of critical friendship among researchers. The discussion highlights the dynamic and nuanced characteristics of our situations as four anti-racist researchers in both geographical spaces and contexts, as well as contemplates strategies for reinforcing collaborative projects among faculty on campus.
Title: Towards anti-racism within higher education: experiencing academia as Black faculty in Brazil and the USA

Abstract: Australia is faced with gendered issues like intimate partner violence and sexual assault which are perpetuated by widespread negative public attitudes that position women as an inferior gender. High-school Relationship and Sex Education (RSE) offers one intervention into these gendered issues. Research shows students dissatisfaction with RSE and gendered inequalities within it. Based on reflections of recent Australian high-school graduates, this study explored the question, what messages about women are communicated through RSE? 12 semi-structured interviews were conducted with Australians (10 women, 2 men) aged 19 to 22 (M=19.58) in 2023 who graduated from high-school in the previous three years. Using critical realist epistemology, an abductive Reflexive Thematic Analysis was conducted, through a postmodern feminist lens. Four themes were constructed: Oversimplified Misrepresentations of Women, The Liable Sex, The Deprioritised Other, and The Virtuous Woman. These themes were supported by a reductive-expansive continuum describing variation in portrayals of women, ranging from rigid traditional conceptualisations to more inclusive, expansive representations. Participants described restrictive, rigid, and outdated gendered messaging. Much messaging about women in RSE reflected problematic attitudes toward women. Shame surfaced as a significant, gendered concept in RSE, particularly affecting women participants; this was explained through Shame Resilience Theory. The reductive-expansive continuum offers a practical framework for evaluating and improving how women are represented in RSE programs. Findings echo calls for comprehensive RSE teacher training and necessitate policy makers and educators to review curricula and reform RSE.
Title: Restricted to the Traditional Female Role: Australian high-school graduates perceptions of the messaging about women in relationship and sex education

Abstract: This article is devoted to the study of the relationship between the conservation of ethno-cultural norms, identities and, the adaptation of forced migrants. Based on the theory of Cumulative (dis)advantage (Dannefer in Social Sci 6:115, 2018), the theory of adaptation and acculturation of migrants (Kim in Communication and Cross-Cultural adaptation: an integrative theory, 1988; Berry et al. in Immigrant youth in cultural transition: acculturation,identity and adaptation across National contexts, 2006), the theory of cultural connectivity (Sani et al. in Eur J Social Psychol 37:11181134, 2007), we assumed that the support from compatriots, the preservation of their own culture, language, and traditions are important parts in the process of adaptation among forced migrants. Both factors the formation of the host society identity and the preservation of identities deriving from their own culture and country of origin are keys to a successful adaptation. This study was conducted among forced migrants from South Ossetia living in Russia. Authors conducted a quantitative survey among  of 412 South Ossetia forced migrants. The results of the structural equation modelling showed that the ethno-cultural norms conservation predicted migrants life satisfaction and socio-cultural adaptation. Additionally, authors found that the conservation of ethno-cultural norms positively associated with ethnic, South Ossetian regional and new Russian national identities. Strong South Ossetian regional identity was related to life satisfaction, and strong new Russian national identity was associated with self-esteem. Additionally, analyses indicated that the conservation of ethno-cultural norms indirectly related to self-esteem through the new Russian national identity.
Title: The adaptation of forced migrants from South Ossetia in Russia: the role of the conservation of ethno-cultural norms, ethnic, regional, and national identities

Abstract: Due to the prevalence of trafficking in human beings and the smuggling of migrants in Africa, attention has often been placed on South-North migration. Thus, human migration, trafficking, and smuggling have dominated the global discourse in recent years thereby putting human trafficking into the mainstream of migration studies. African Union (AU) has through various policy frameworks tried to criminalise and prosecute those involved in human trafficking and human smuggling in Africa. Despite various AU migration regimes to curb irregular migrations and human trafficking, trafficking in persons and smuggling of migrants have not abated. The article argued that traffickers and smugglers leverage on lack of harmonisation of the non-binding migration policy frameworks among AU member states to embark upon both regular and irregular migration across the state and regional borders to traffic and smuggle migrants to Europe and other destinations. The conclusion, therefore, is that AU migration policy frameworks have little impact on the campaign against human trafficking in Africa in terms of abating trafficking in persons. This has ensured that the notorious Niger/Chad/Nigeria borders have remained the Triangle of Shame. This article is essentially a desktop study relying on qualitative analysis of secondary sources and a rigorous review of policy documents.
Title: The Triangle of Shame: interrogating the impact of African Union migration policy frameworks on human trafficking in Africa

Abstract: Tanzanias implementation of fee-free secondary education was an essential intervention that provided opportunity and improved access to and participation in education. Evidence suggests that removing mandatory contributions and school fees has led to a rise in enrolment. Using human capital and human-right theoretical perspectives, this qualitative-based study was carried out in Tanzania to explore how fee-free secondary education contributes to students academic persistence, focusing on school enrolment, issues and the challenges facing parents and students when enrolling in secondary schools. Data was generated by focus group discussions, interviews and observation with parents, teachers, students and district officers. Findings revealed that fee-free secondary education increased enrolment for both boys and girls and students from low and marginalized households. However, cultural norms, the cost of education, and poverty in the households hampered the enrolment. The study concludes that removing mandatory parental contributions and tuition fees is not only a panacea to realise improved quality education provision and delivery as delayed entry and not enrolling negates the goal for which fee-free education was introduced. The study recommends that a complementary intervention that specifically targets offsetting direct costs and improving household income may be necessary for fee-free education to reap the fruits. In addition, more concerted efforts and community sensitisation about the importance of investing in education are still needed to address knock-on challenges.
Title: The contributions of fee-free secondary education to students academic persistence in Tanzania: patterns, problems and possibilities

Abstract: As travellers move across different jurisdictions and their data are extensively utilized, privacy protection has become even more paramount in the tourism industry. The aim of this study is to examine how data protection, data security, data breach prevention and data policies affect international tourists destination referral intentions. The study was grounded on the optimism and pessimism theory utilizing the convenience sampling method through a self-reporting questionnaire to collect primary data from 426 international tourists. The results of the hypotheses showed that data protection, data breach prevention, data policy are significant predictors of destination referral from international tourists perspective. However, the data security was not a significant predictor of destination referral in context. The study sheds light on the optimism and pessimism theory, from the quantitative findings that data protection, data breach prevention, data policy are optimistic factors that influenced destination referral.
Title: International tourists data privacy and destination referral: Ghanas perspective

Abstract: Since the advent of democracy in South Africa, the education system has endeavoured to ensure not only physical access but also epistemological access to learning for all students. Consequently, the imperative of basic education is to deliver a curriculum that is equitable and inclusive. Higher education institutions teacher education programs serve as crucial social agents capable of driving transformative curricula grounded in a framework of social justice. This study seeks to explore the potential of decolonizing pre-service teacher education for equity and inclusivity through socially just pedagogies (SJPs). The curriculum under examination revitalizes SJPs, emphasizing the significance of personal pedagogical dimensions, the politics of difference, and the nexus between pedagogy and agency. Through interviews with nine purposively selected curriculum studies lecturers across all three North-West University campuses in South Africa, we elucidate how SJPs can inform a more equitable and inclusive curriculum aligned with transformative ideals. Lecturers advocate for the integration of new concepts/topics in teacher education to advance the transformation of knowledge, power, and identity within the curriculum. They call for the recognition and incorporation of Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS), history, and languages to achieve equity and inclusivity in curriculum delivery. This study contributes to the discourse by amplifying voices from the Global South that challenge the predominant Eurocentric learning paradigm in South Africa and offer an alternative perspective on decolonized pre-service teacher education through SJPs.
Title: Rethinking teacher development: blending socially responsible teaching approaches with Indigenous Knowledge to enhance equity and inclusivity

Abstract: The endurance of civilizations is shaped not by technological progress alone, but by governance, social cohesion (asabiyyah), and ecological stewardship. This study revisits Ibn Khalduns climatic framework, drawing fromThe Muqaddimahto explore the temperate, intemperate, and intermediate zones, linking his insights to contemporary urban sustainability. Through the case examples of Stockholm, Dubai, and Phoenix, the paper examines how governance models either align with or defy environmental realities. While Stockholm integrates sustainability within its climatic conditions, Dubai and Phoenix rely on high-energy interventions, raising concerns about long-term resilience. Supported by scholarly research, the findings suggest that sustainability is not merely an engineering challenge but a civilizational imperative, demanding a balance between ambition and restraint, innovation and justice. Ibn Khalduns insights offer a historically grounded alternative to technocratic models, providing a multidimensional framework for fostering resilient, equitable, and sustainable cities in an era of climate change and rapid urbanization.
Title: Integrating Ibn Khalduns wisdom into urban sustainability

Abstract: The social, economic, and environmental health of cities relies on the effective and efficient management of its natural assets such as green spaces. Cities in the developing world are still experiencing uncontrolled urbanization, which poses a threat to the sustainability of green spaces. In this study, the researchers present the classification of green spaces in Kumasi using Swanwick et al.s (Built Environ 29(2):94106, 2003) categorisation of green spaces. Additionally, the researchers assessed the factors that threaten the sustainability of these green spaces. The study used a mixed methods approach, interviewing 345 green space users and their managers and conducting spatial analysis on green cover. The findings indicate a significant reduction in green cover by 39.86% between 2013 and 2023 due to urban expansion. Study results further showed that green spaces such as the KNUST Botanical Garden, the Royal Parade Ground, the Owabi Wildlife Sanctuary, and the Ahodwo Roundabout to Kumasi Metropolitan Assembly Clinic Road Corridor can be categorized into amenity green space, functional green space, semi-natural green space, and linear green space, respectively. The study revealed that green space categories determine users, uses, and management strategies. Threats to green space sustainability include encroachment, poor maintenance, and unsustainable funding. Urgent policy reform and innovative urban planning strategies are needed to ensure sustainable green space management.
Title: The functionality of urban green spaces in the greater Kumasi Metropolis of Ghana: categorisation of green spaces, prospects, challenges and implications for sustainable management

Abstract: An assessment by the World Health Organization found that climate change since the 1970s was causing over 140,000 excess deaths annually with developing countries contributing minimally to climate change. Ironically, these countries are disproportionately affected by the negative health impacts of climate change. To shed light on this paradox, the present study investigates climate change and its effect on health outcomes in Sub-Saharan African countries during the period from 2004 to 2019. Using the Driscoll-Kraay fixed effect and the two-step system Generalized Method of Moments regressions, the study finds that climate change significantly worsens health outcomes. Specifically, the prevalence of undernourishment, infant mortality rate, and malaria incidence are positively and significantly influenced by various climate change indicators. All else equal, a 1-unit rise in surface temperature increases undernourishment by 0.183, infant mortality by 0.363, and malaria incidence by 9.658. Conversely, life expectancy at birth is negatively and significantly affected with a 1-unit rise in surface temperature reducing life expectancy at birth by 0.129years. This imply that as climate change becomes more pronounced, health risks increase substantially, leading to a reduction in life expectancy. The results are validated through various robustness checks, and based on the findings, the study recommends the development and implementation of comprehensive climate-resilient healthcare strategies.
Title: Climate change and its effect on health outcomes: an empirical investigation of Sub-Saharan Africa countries

Abstract: This study aims to assess the legal framework for child protection in South Asia, evaluate the progress made, and identify prevailing obstacles. To achieve this, the research employs the Meta Analysis of the Search, Appraisal, Synthesis, and Analysis (SALSA) framework, conducting a systematic review of UNICEFs primary data on child protection legislation in the region. The Scopus search results revealed a limited number of published documents on child protection and related areas, with only seven of them being relevant and providing some coverage of child protection in South Asia. The analysis uncovers significant progress in establishing legal measures to safeguard childrens rights. However, it also highlights persistent challenges, including weak enforcement mechanisms, legal gaps, resource constraints, cultural barriers, and limited awareness. These findings can serve as valuable insights for policymakers, practitioners, and advocates in South Asia. By building upon successful initiatives and effectively addressing obstacles, they can foster regional collaboration to strengthen child protection systems, ultimately ensuring a safer and more secure environment for children in the region.
Title: Child protection in South Asia: assessing the current status, progress, and obstacles of the legal framework

Abstract: The effective application of urban design principles relies on the enforcement of planning regulations, guidelines, and standards. While scholars globally have examined compliance and non-compliance with these regulations, this study seeks to improve existing knowledge by studying the phenomenon from the perspective of professional planners in the Ghanaian context. Planning practitioners are key stakeholders in the planning process and are therefore vital in helping to achieve the sustainable development goals especially Goal 11 which seeks to ensure sustainable cities and communities. Therefore, understanding their insights on the implications of non-compliance with planning regulations for the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals is of great relevance to the sustainability and urban planning literature. In this study, a total of 47 planning professionals were interviewed from twelve (12) Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs) in the Ashanti Region of Ghana. The study found that non-compliance with planning regulations in the study region has led to the creation of slums, pollution of water, and encroachment in ecologically sensitive areas. These have implications for the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly Goals 1, 6, and 11. There is the urgent need to revise the building permitting process by selling the service to developers instead of waiting for developers to patronize the service.
Title: Non-compliance with planning regulations and their implication for the achievement of the sustainable development goals: insights from physical planners in the Ashanti Region of Ghana

Abstract: Studies depict that early childhood programs which are based on indigenous knowledge are more valuable than the Western traditions for young children. Keeping this all-in mind, the present study is aimed at exploring the role of IK in early childhood education, particularly in numeracy development. It aims to fill the knowledge gap in indigenous early childhood education and contribute to the literature and policy on the subject. The study uses a mixed-methods approach, involving 30 elders and 30 children from the Sidama people in Ethiopia. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and questionnaire. The findings reveal that the Sidama peoples indigenous games, such asTiiki-tiikiyyo,Hayyye,Assitta-assumma,and Shilingeya bau, teach young children early numeracy skills. These games involve activities that help children count numbers, identify shapes, and compare objects. However, the study also found that many indigenous knowledge and practices are not well incorporated into early childhood practices. Therefore, the study suggests the need for further in-depth investigations in this area. The expected outcomes were to identify the benefits and challenges of using IK in early childhood care and education, develop a framework for incorporating IK into the numeracy curriculum and pedagogy, and provide insights into the role of indigenous games in promoting numeracy development and cultural diversity in ECCE.
Title: Indigenous knowledge and its contribution to early childhood numeracy development

Abstract: Despite being an essential part of the urban environment, access nuances of the Central Business District (CBD), a very critical space in cities of the Global South are not well-explained in the extant literature. Therefore, this study used Kumasi Central as a case to explore space access, user experiences, and dominant access means. The study used semi-structured interviews to collect data from eighty- one respondents from eight permissible CBD use cohorts and 5 experts from city management institutions. According to the results, the mechanisms to access space in Central Kumasi are money, social and cultural connections, and ties to government officials. However, out of the four means, money is the most predominant. The research finds affirmation for the predominance of money through its appreciation as the force, fuel, driver, and lifeline to secure a place in the CBD. Thus, lack of money seriously refutes access to a secured space in the CBD. The study reveals that even though possessing social and cultural connections, and links to state personnel facilitate access, these means are limited to a privileged few. As a result, the study infers that access politics is an experiential reality with implications for exclusions to crucial spaces for cities of emerging countries. Consequently, the study recommends that adopting a collaborative and participatory approach informed by real time data on localised experiences in the formulation and implementation of advocative policies may support spatially redistributive and transformational initiatives. Again, access politics contain psychosomatic components; as such, research may go further to model it in addition to the inescapably physical and obvious access dynamics.
Title: Access politics in an emerging economy: evidence from central Kumasi

Abstract: The primary objective of this study is to examine the effectiveness of institutional factors on economic crime in two regions, backward (BOMARU) and forward (South-West) in India from 1994 to 2018. Economic crime included Breach of Trust, Cheating, Counterfeiting, and forgery. Institutional factors include the police and court which are fear factors. Data have been taken from the National Crime Record Bureau in India (NCRB) and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Handbook 2011. Panel data analysis, particularly the Fixed Effect model has been applied for the purpose. The result reveals that financial development may control economic crime whereas institutional factor has no significant role in controlling crime in the forward region (South-West). Institutional factors play a vibrant role in controlling crime in the backward region (BOMARU). Financial development should be strengthened to mitigate crime in the forward region and institutional factors should be strengthened to control crime in the backward region in India.
Title: Effectiveness of institutional factors on economic crime in forward and backward regions of India: an empirical analysis

Abstract: This qualitative study used a case study approach to explore the technology professional development of teacher educators in Malawi, examining four cases. The research focused on three key questions: How do teacher educators in Malawi engage in technology professional learning? What technological skills do they learn? Why do they pursue technology professional learning? Findings revealed that while teacher educators are motivated to enhance their technology competencies, the content of their professional development often lacks a focus on their specific professional roles, such as preparing future educators or modelling teaching practices. A key cultural issue influencing these findings may lie in how teacher educators conceptualise technology. This perspective may limit the scope of professional development, emphasising technical skills over broader pedagogical uses. The study highlights the importance of considering institutional and individual-level factors when implementing national teacher education standards. It also calls for further research into the role of research, community of practice, and mentoring in technology competencies, as well as a deeper exploration of how these practices vary across diverse educational contexts in Malawi.
Title: How, What and Why do teacher educators in Malawi learn about technology?

Abstract: Over the years, public procurement has gained attention among researchers and practitioners from diverse geographical areas owing to its notoriety as a conduit for corruption. Many studies have examined the subject of public procurement corruption (PPC), nevertheless, studies on the present and future trends in PPC research in developing countries are still patchy. This affected our understanding of the trends and issues in PPC studies in this context. Therefore, this study comprehensively reviews the trends in PPC in developing countries and provides directions for future studies. The study employed the Scientometric approach to analyse 152 documents from the Scopus database. The study unearthed the trends in the PPC domain, the most influential and prolific journals, authors, countries, institutions, and the co-occurrence network of keywords. Besides, the qualitative analysis revealed various themes in PPC studies namely: procurement-based corruption, procurement strategies and corruption, public procurement and corruption, bidder selection and corruption, preventative and remedial measures (accountability, transparency, technology, laws and regulations), gender and corruption, etc. This study adds to the body of knowledge in PPC studies by furnishing scholars with the trends and future avenues in PPC studies. Furthermore, this study arms practitioners and policymakers with some procurement mitigation strategies that can be used to reduce the menace of PPC, thereby promoting national development and alleviating poverty.
Title: Public procurement corruption in developing countries context: a review and research agenda

Abstract: A secure Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) environment indicates safe and healthy human life and safeguards womens dignity and privacy. Usually, women are responsible for household WASH management along with Menstrual Hygienic Services (MHS). In this context, our study aims to distinguish the contemporary condition of Womens Empowerment (WE) and WASH and the influence of WE on WASH, including Safely Managed Drinking Water (SMW), Safely Managed Sanitation (SMS), Basic Hygiene Services (BHS), and Menstrual Hygiene Services (MHS) in India. The study utilizes the fifth National Family Health Survey of India from the Demographic Health Survey (DHS) of 20192021. The study uses descriptive statistics, bivariate scatter plots, Pearsons correlation coefficient, bivariate LISA (Local indicators of spatial autocorrelation), and Morans I. Results from the study reflect that the districts from south, west, north, and northeast Indian states have an improved position in WE, SMW, and BHS. Meanwhile, the districts from south, west, and southeast states are better in SMS, and the districts from north, south, and northeast states are better in MHS. Pearsons correlation coefficient shows a slight positive relation between SMW and SMS with WE; it is deplorable for BHS. The relationship between MHS and WE is relatively strong and positive, indicating that an empowered woman can control her menstrual practices more than the household WASH conditions. The study will help planners and the government implement policies in the backward areas of WE and WASH. Thus, the study will also accomplish SDG-5 (gender equality) by enhancing WE and SDG-6 (WASH) by improving availability, affordability, accessibility, and awareness of WASH facilities.
Title: Womens empowerment and water, sanitation, and hygiene in India: exploring the present situation and correlation using geostatistical techniques

Abstract: Artificial intelligence in education is touted as transformative and is promoted to solve the higher education crises. The latest developments in artificial intelligence, in the form of Generative Artificial Intelligence, garnered much research and policy interest. In particular, it holds strong promises for teachers by assisting them in customising and personalising learning, providing real-time feedback on students assessments, and enriching professional training. These merits particularly become crucial for a developing nation like India, where there seems to be a lack of interactive learning in traditional classrooms due to a high pupil-teacher ratio, amongst other reasons. However, there is a dearth of literature studying teachers competencies in adopting generative artificial intelligence, particularly in light of the Technology, Pedagogy, and Content knowledge framework Mishra (J Digit Learn Teacher Educ 39(4):235-251, 2023). This study fills this gap by offering a parsimonious 20-item scale named the Gen AIHE-TPACK scale to examine higher education teachers competencies in developing and emerging economies following the six-fold methodology of scale development and validation. The scale is validated based on the survey results from a sample of 181 college teachers. The proposed scale can be used by policymakers and academicians to better assess teachers competencies in the era of artificial intelligence.
Title: Examining teachers competencies in generative AI-enabled higher education: scale development and validation for empirical research

Abstract: COVID-19 has emerged as a global catastrophe, causing substantial repercussions worldwide, particularly in developing countries. This study aims to investigate the consequences of the COVID-19-induced lockdown on vulnerable rural communities in the Kushtia district of Bangladesh, with a specific focus on their coping strategies. Using a qualitative approach, the study analyzed data from 48 in-depth interviews, 4 focus group discussions (FGDs), and 14 key informant interviews (KIIs) through thematic analysis. The study reveals that rural communities in the Kushtia district experienced significant impacts due to the COVID-19-induced lockdown, including economic, food, health, and educational repercussions. Additionally, the situation has deteriorated over time due to the ongoing transmission of COVID-19. The study also uncovered various coping strategies employed by these rural communities, such as borrowing money and food, utilizing savings, selling and mortgaging assets, and reducing meals and expenses. The study recommends prioritizing economic aid and enhancing food distribution systems to alleviate financial strain and food insecurity, while advocating for scalable health and education interventions to build resilience against future crises.
Title: Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on vulnerable communities and their coping strategies: evidence from Kushtia district, Bangladesh

Abstract: Securing Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) sustainability in the future of work is highly threatened by a host of occupational safety and health management problems. Without adoption of pragmatic and systematic interventions to address these problems, attainment of sustainable development in line with Agenda 2030 will remain a pipedream. The study aimed at developing a model for improved implementation of OSH management systems (OSHMSs) in the manufacturing industry of Mutare. A descriptive cross-sectional study design was utilized. Collection of primary data was done through administration of questionnaires, interviews and the OSHMS assessment matrix whilst secondary data sources included targeted companies OSH records and documents, past OSH research papers and internet-based OSH databases. Results show that provision of personal protective clothing and equipment is the most implemented element of an OSHMS in the manufacturing industry of Mutare. The designed Model for improved OSHMSs implementation in the manufacturing industry of Mutare is a major output of this study. The model demonstrates the inter-dependability of various stakeholders at national, strategic, and operational levels in the equation for improved implementation of OSHMSs. It can be deduced from the model that improved OHSMS implementation cannot be achieved by a simple mono-causal intervention hence an ecosystem of intervention is needed to attain sustainability in OSHMSs implementation. Total commitment of Government and its social partners and other OSH stakeholders, the participation and involvement of workers and the continual adaptation to changing circumstances are paramount for the realization of the ambition to improve implementation of OSHMSs at workplaces.
Title: A context based model for improved implementation of occupational safety and health management systems in mutare manufacturing industry, Zimbabwe

Abstract: This study examines the persistent sanitation challenges and public health concerns in Sodom and Gomorrah, the largest slum in Accra, Ghana. Using a phenomenological qualitative approach, the research explores the lived experiences of residents to understand how inadequate sanitation infrastructure, poor waste disposal practices, and socio-economic inequalities exacerbate public health risks. The findings highlight the prevalence of diseases such as malaria, cholera, and genitourinary infections, driven by a lack of access to clean water, proper waste management systems, and sanitary facilities. Additionally, the study accentuates the role of information dynamics in shaping sanitation behaviors and public health outcomes. Applying Mindsponge Theory, the research reveals how residents process, prioritize, and act upon sanitation-related information amidst competing survival priorities. The study emphasizes the importance of reducing informational entropyuncertainty and inconsistency in health messagesand delivering contextually relevant, culturally sensitive information to promote sustainable hygiene practices. It advocates for a rights-based, participatory governance approach that integrates community-driven sanitation solutions with systemic infrastructure improvements. The study contributes to the broader discourse on urban slums by linking sanitation and public health issues to socio-economic and informational dynamics, providing actionable recommendations for policymakers, urban planners, and public health practitioners. These include enhancing sanitation infrastructure, leveraging local social networks for effective information dissemination, and addressing structural inequalities to foster resilience in marginalized communities. By framing Sodom and Gomorrahs challenges within a global context, this research offers insights into creating sustainable urban environments aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goals 3, 6, and 11.
Title: Sanitation struggles and public health concerns in Ghana: insights from Sodom and Gomorrah slum

Abstract: Informal, authentic STEM learning enhances PK-12 students knowledge, attitudes, and interests, but field-based contexts remain underexplored. This study investigated how an authentic Journalism, Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (JSTEM) Program impacted Latinx high schoolers science/engineering skills, practices, knowledge, STEM attitudes/interests, and transfer of informal learning to formal settings. Using a case study approach, students participated in the JSTEM programs field-based authentic STEM activities. Data sources included assessments, observations, interviews, and student artifacts. The approach enhanced learning of science/engineering practices, fostered positive STEM attitudes/interests, and facilitated transfer to formal environments. Students demonstrated improved skills, knowledge, and heightened interests/attitudes, and applied informal concepts formally. The study highlights the potential of informal, authentic STEM learning opportunities to engage and inspire students, particularly those from underrepresented groups. Incorporating authentic, hands-on activities can foster STEM identity, belongingness, and preparedness for STEM careers and further education.
Title: Engaging Latinx students in scientific inquiry and metacognition through authentic STEM experiences

Abstract: Midwife continuity of carer (MCOC) is widely recommended to protect birthing people against disrespectful care and mitigate effects of social adversity. In the UK, this is reflected in the Core20PLUS5 framework, which identifies maternity and, specifically, MCOC as one of five national priorities for reducing healthcare inequalities. Within health policy networks, the prevailing view of the policy process is that the task of government is to find solutions to existing policy problems. A critical policy approach, in contrast, considers how any policy proposal represents a problem in a particular way, shaping what is perceived as possible or desirable. Adopting this approach, I suggest that the promise of MCOC (and, specifically, intrapartum continuity) has been overstated, given the context of extreme social inequality, chronic underfunding of the NHS, the impact of austerity and the denial of structural racism in the UK. MCOC has been found to improve access, experience, and outcomes for disadvantaged and racially minoritized people by offering more personalized care. When MCOC is the policy proposal, however, the problem of inequalities in perinatal health tends to be represented in terms of fragmented maternity care, limiting policy discussion of the drivers of health inequality. This enables elected officials to appear to address health inequality by relying on midwives to adopt more flexible working practices. Representing the problem as a matter of health justice, in contrast, not only requires that personalized care is informed by structural competency and cultural safety but demands that policymakers address structural drivers beyond the healthcare system.
Title: When midwife continuity of carer is the policy proposal, what is the problem of perinatal health inequalities represented to be?

Abstract: This mixed-methods study examined mental health challenges and coping strategies among working class academics (WCAs) in the UK. Data was collected over five years (20182023) through interviews (n=163) and a survey (n=90) of WCAs. Three primary factors contributing to mental health challenges were identified: 1. economic insecurity, 2. imposter syndrome, and 3. cultural disconnection. These factors were associated with increased stress, anxiety, and depression among WCAs. Despite these challenges, WCAs demonstrated resilience through three key strategies: 1. embracing working-class identity as a strength, 2. adaptability, and persistence, and 3. building supportive networks. This study highlights persistent class-based obstacles in academia, challenging narratives about educations transformative power and extending understanding of imposter syndrome by linking it to class background. Findings inform policies for inclusive academic environments, suggesting targeted mental health support, professional development, financial aid, and inclusion of class in diversity initiatives. Future research directions include comparative studies on WCA-specific challenges, longitudinal research on career trajectories, and asset-based approaches to leveraging class diversity in academia. This study underscores the urgent need for systemic changes to address classism and promote equity in HE.
Title: Working class academics and mental health: challenges and coping strategies

Abstract: Crises such as armed conflicts and natural disasters usually have harmful effects on childrens education. However, they may also make the public more aware of the importance of education. During times of crisis, more people may realize that a good education helps to maintain or regain employment and earnings. Consequently, crises may raise the publics educational prioritization. To test this hypothesis, the paper uses data on six types of crisis covering 50 countries. The types of crisis studied are natural disasters, internal and external conflicts as well as unemployment, inflation and banking crises. The regression results show that each type of crisis is associated with higher educational prioritization, corroborating the hypothesis. Except for unemployment crises, the magnitude of the estimated effects is substantial. The paper combines individual-level data from the World Values Survey with country-level data on crises and relevant national characteristics.
Title: Crises and educational prioritization

Abstract: Research has now well documented that minoritized individuals, particularly Blacks, are more likely to be victims of police use of force in the United States. However, the various social and physical environments in which racial/ethnic minority victimization is more likely to occur remain poorly understood. Some evidence has suggested that a higher percentage of minorities in residential space and racial/ethnic residential segregation are both related to a higher rate of police use of force. Here, we examine how spatial clustering of Black, Latino, and White residents relate to both fatal and non-fatal police use of force using data at both the national level and in a subset analysis of Texas. We find that Black and Latino clustering are related to higher rates of overall fatal and non-fatal police use of force, as well as higher rates of both Black and Latino victimization respectively. However, the opposite is the case for White clustering. White clustering across neighborhoods is negatively related to both fatal and non-fatal police use of force. Moreover, when broken out by race, White clustering is unrelated to the White victimization rate. These patterns suggest that White neighborhoods are relatively advantaged spaces when the police interact with civilians.
Title: White residential clustering, race/ethnicity, and police use of force across neighborhoods in the United States

Abstract: The Muni-Pomadze Lagoon in Winneba, Ghana, is an important ecosystem that underpins biodiversity, water purification, and livelihoods. The research evaluates how urban sprawl together with encroachment affects the size of the lagoon along with its water quality and biodiversity standing. It also examines current conservation strategies effectiveness. The study adopted a mixed-method approach, which combined quantitative surveys of 80 respondents with in-depth interviews and focus group discussions. Regression analysis of lagoon shrinkage showed that the size of the lagoon has been decreasing by 2.5% annually, which is equal to 25% loss within a decade (R = 1.000,p<0.0001). Water quality seriously deteriorated, with a 4-unit annual rise in pollution level, a 200% rise since 2013 (R = 1.000,p<0.0001). Biodiversity was reduced by 40%, the number of species decreased from 50 to 30 over the same period. Strong correlations were found between lagoon degradation and population growth (r=0.92,p<0.01) and infrastructure developments (r=0.89,p<0.01), and residual analysis singled out weak policy enforcement as a key unaccounted factor. The highlighted inadequate conservation efforts, poor zoning enforcement, and poor community awareness of the role in this decrease. Current measures, such as buffer zones, have proven inadequate. Without intervention, projections indicate an additional 15% loss in lagoon size and further biodiversity loss by 2033. It is, therefore, a call for the enforcement of zoning laws to the letter, increased funding for conservation, community initiatives, and adaptive management practices. Integration of urban planning with ecological preservation is very important to arrest this trend of degradation. These findings have increased the need for integrated policies that balance urban development with the sustainability of Ghanas coastal wetlands, ensuring long-term ecosystem services and community resilience.
Title: Assessing the impacts of urban sprawl and encroachment on Muni-Pomadze Lagoon ecosystem at Winneba, Ghana

Abstract: This study aims to investigate how the selection of data sources affects the assessment of progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Using the Kyrgyz Republic as a case study, this research addresses an often-overlooked issue in sustainable development monitoring: national and global data can paint conflicting pictures of progress. Methodologically, the study compares national statistics from the Kyrgyz National Statistical Committee (NSC) with global SDG data from the Sustainable Development Report (SDR) to identify discrepancies in reported outcomes. A three-step approach ensures a comprehensive analysis: first, we examine time-series data for SDG targets and indicators, second, we compare raw data between SDR and NSC databases, and third analyze and compare SDG progress indices across the two data sources. Key findings reveal that the country has made notable improvements in several goals (e.g., SDGs 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, and 11), but faces persistent challenges in others, notably SDGs 5 and 16. A comparison of progress indices between NSC and SDR data shows that nine goals (SDGs 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 16) demonstrate conflicting trends at the global and national levels, highlighting the critical importance of using accurate, harmonized data to monitor progress toward the SDGs and plan future actions to achieve them. Decision-makers must be aware of these discrepancies to ensure proper resource allocation and effective planning for achieving the SDGs.
Title: Why does data selection matter in tracking progress toward Sustainable Development Goals?

Abstract: Over 89 million people are forcefully displaced and are living as refugees away from their homes. Humanitarian energy is registered as one of the critical needs affecting both the refugees and host communities. The study aimed to comprehensively review existing literature to identify the definitions of humanitarian energy, the interventions, and the barriers to scaling such interventions. The study adopted a systematic literature approach to identify, evaluate, and select primary journal articles and grey literature using pre-determined inclusion and exclusion criteria. In so doing, the right articles were identified and included for synthesis in the study. The review identified several definitions of humanitarian energy. interventions and barriers to the scaling up of the interventions. We recommended that organizations operating in humanitarian energy create partnerships rather than working in isolation. In addition, there is a need to provide programmes that build the humanitarian energy providers and the refugees capacity.
Title: Sustainable humanitarian energy transitions: a review of interventions and challenges

Abstract: Across the twentieth century, sociologist Emory Bogardus conducted several pioneering national surveys of social distance attitudes in the United States, documenting how various ancestry groups were viewed by those in the larger society as desirable candidates for close social relationships. These surveys hint that the English, Scots, and Irish  ancestries that respondents viewed as most desirable in the early twentieth century  declined in favorability by the late twentieth century. This decline infers that the relatively high status of these British Isles ancestry groups was moderated by group-identity shifts and modernization. The present studys ANOVA explores this possibility, neglect in past research, with Bogardus data. As expected, Scottish or Irish ancestry persons were viewed less favorably than White Americans in later surveys. Yet, unexpectedly, English ancestry persons favorability equaled that of White Americans across all surveys. The study concludes that uniquely favorable views of English ancestry are more firmly ingrained into U.S. culture than group-identification and societal modernization theories suggest.
Title: Social distance attitudes toward British Isles ancestry groups in the twentieth-century United States: persistence, change, and historical legacy

Abstract: This research investigates the impacts of gender and geographical settings on the relationship between mobile phone ownership and cycling behaviour in Ghana. The paper used probit regression to analyse data from 12,855 households. The findings revealed that both mobile phone ownership and males significantly positively influence cycling behaviour. The gender and geographical settings of household heads reinforced this association, with urban men who own mobile phones more likely to engage in cycling than urban women. In addition, while the likelihood of cycling varies across all regions, the findings showed that the highest of the likelihoods came from the Northern, Upper West, and East regions. Furthermore, the results indicated that while radio ownership and family size have positive links with cycling behaviour, the level of education and wealth status of the household heads have significant negative associations with cycling behaviour. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the value of considering gender and geographical settings when understanding the relationship between mobile phone ownership and cycling behaviour. The findings have policy, theoretical, and practical implications for promoting sustainable transportation and environmental goals in Ghana.
Title: Impacts of gender and geographical settings on the relationship between mobile phone ownership and cycling behaviour in Ghana

Abstract: Women in every society face various forms of physical, psychological and economic exploitation, often leading to their marginalization and exclusion from social and cultural life. This study attempts to explore the trends and patterns of crimes against women (CAW) in the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir over five years (20182022), highlighting spatial and temporal variations across districts. Unlike previous studies that focus on individual crimes or socio-economic factors, this research employs advanced spatial analysis techniques, including Morans I for spatial autocorrelation and Getis-Ord Gi* for hotspot detection, to examine the clustering and spillover effects of crimes such as rape, dowry deaths, and cruelty by husbands or relatives. The findings indicate distribution of CAW, with districts like Baramulla, Srinagar, Jammu, and Budgam continuously recognised as hotspots, while Pulwama and Rajouri have recently exhibited rising crime rates. This indicates that CAW is no longer confined to a limited number of districts but is dispersed throughout the region. By integrating geographical distribution, temporal trends, and the regions unique socio-political context, this study provides actionable insights for region-specific crime prevention policies and a nuanced understanding of how spatial dynamics influence womens safety.
Title: Mapping the geography of crime against women in the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir: a Geospatial analysis

Abstract: Loktak Lake, a Ramsar wetland, is under tremendous threat of ecological deterioration, which causes biodiversity loss and perils the livelihood of fisherfolk. The study aims to examine the ecological risks in fishing and the livelihood strategies of the fisherfolk in response to ecological change. It also focuses on migration from fishers community and investigates factors influencing the likelihood of labour migration through a case-controlled study. It comprises qualitative and quantitative techniquesparticipatory risk mapping (PRM) to measure subjective risks, thematic mapping (TM) using conversational artificial intelligence (AI) based on key informant interviews, and a Binary Logistic Regression model (BLR) based on the Sustainable Livelihood Approach (SLA). The study finds that ecological risks, such asphumdiproliferation, water pollution, declining fish species and production, lowering depth, and submergence of farmlands, are grave concerns among fisherfolk and significantly affect their livelihood. Compared to non-ecological risks, ecological issues have been portrayed predominantly in PRM of fishers in terms of wider concern and greater impact. AI-based TM portrays that fisherfolk follow various livelihood strategies, including job transformation, diversification, and migration, which is most predominantthree from every two households. Migration has double benefitsit declines pressure on natural resources and facilitates conservation, vis--vis, reduces economic hardship. Conserving ecology and sustainable fishing practices is a prerequisite for sustainable livelihood for fisherfolk. An inclusive approach to resource management is essential to ensure the locals participation in the conservation process in a large, sustainable usage of natural resources and coordination of multiple sectors and stakeholders.
Title: Ecological change, livelihood issues and migration- a study on fisherfolk in Ramsar Wetland, Loktak lake in India

Abstract: In this paper, critical variables in participatory research are addressed from a multidisciplinary perspective on the basis of experiences from previous research projects in educational sciences, psychology, and sociology. An overview of multidisciplinary perspectives on participatory research is provided, including key factors for (successful) participatory processes on an individual and collective level. With that, we aim to stimulate future research on participatory processes between science and practice by identifying critical success factors that might be crucial in research planning, implementation and evaluation of multidisciplinary participatory processes. This multidisciplinary approach should also help academic researchers from other disciplines to implement multidisciplinary participatory research.
Title: Multidisciplinary perspectives on participatory research projects of educational sciences, psychology and sociology: reflections about critical factors

Abstract: The influence of anthropogenic and natural driving forces has resulted in a remarkable change in vegetation cover in Bangladesh in recent years. This study explored the changes in vegetation cover and their driving forces in the Shibganj sub-district of Chapainawabganj district, Bangladesh, from 1990 to 2020. The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) was employed to analyse the changes in vegetation cover, while a qualitative study explored the underlying driving forces. The results (image analysis) showed a considerable shift in vegetation land cover, with an increase of 180.68 square kilometre (sq. km.) between 1990 and 2020, and 128.37 sq. km. between 2000 and 2020. Additionally, a qualitative study indicated that climatic and hydrological conditions, alongside several economic, technological, and institutional factors, were the major driving forces of these changes. Moreover, mango farming has increased by 108.5 sq. km. over the last two decades, owing to minimal water requirements, ideal agro-environmental conditions, and high commercial demand. The data indicate that the transition from conventional food grain production to mango farming has contributed to an overall increase in vegetation cover in this moderately drought-prone region. This study sheds light on how natural and manmade variables influence land use and vegetation dynamics.
Title: Detecting vegetation change and exploring its driving forces in North-western region of Bangladesh

Abstract: Land and property rights are crucial for development, yet access and security remain obstacles in many parts of the global south, including Ghana. This study examines the dimensions of perceived property protection (PPP) in Ghana across different socioeconomic and institutional conditions. Using data from the 2020 Global Land Alliance Prindex Baseline Survey on Ghana with 1455 respondents, the research investigates issues surrounding PPP through closed, open-ended, and semi-structured questionnaires analyzed via non-parametric statistics. The results reveal that Ghanaians perceive their rights to land and property security to be secured. The perceived security is influenced by factors such as the right to dwelling, marital status, asset ownership, knowledge of arbitration, and authority support. However, the perceived risk of losing a dwelling upon spousal death or divorce is high, reinforcing patriarchal cultural norms that disadvantage womens access to property. This study contributes insights into the multidimensional nature of perceived land rights and tenure security in Ghana.
Title: Dimensions of perceived land rights and security of property in Ghana

Abstract: This paper addresses the potential social risk associated with the capability to infer sensitive opinions from large self-reported data within a computational-intensive world, in which AI is pervasively and inherently adopted as part of the resulting socio-technical system. Such a social risk should be framed assuming a variety of socio-political contexts, including also non-democratic systems or, more in general, systems with significant lacks in terms of human rights. A simplified view of social risk is considered proportional to the sensitivity of the information and the prediction performance. The related computational experiments are conducted by applying Machine Learning techniques (Neural Networks) on a pre-existent case study based on a subset of the popular World Values Survey. Despite such a use case is not explicitly designed to maximise the prediction performance and is characterised by low dimensionality, the empirical results pointed out an overall interesting capability to infer potentially sensitive information. Additionally, the prediction accuracy resulted to be proportional to the likelihood of data to change along the time. Those results are discussed in context in the paper, looking holistically at the associated social risk, as well as at possible practical implications. In a continuously evolving context, characterised by fast advances of AI technology in contrast with a lack of systematic frameworks for reasoning about risk, uncertainty, and their potentially catastrophic consequences, this study focuses on computational experimentation and case studies to further stimulate the convergence of analysis frameworks and to nurture awareness from both a social and a user perspective.
Title: Addressing the potential social risk of self-reported data within a computational-intensive world

Abstract: Human security challenges in the Global South present significant obstacles to sustainable development and well-being, particularly for vulnerable populations. Despite the critical nature of these issues, there is a noticeable lack of comprehensive studies in this region examining human security across all its domains. It underscores the urgent need for a thorough investigation into human security in the Global South. Employing a structured methodology based on the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) framework, this review systematically synthesises empirical studies across the seven key domains of human security. The findings highlight a concerning rise in human security challenges, disproportionately affecting women, children, refugees, people living in poverty, and marginalised communities. These groups face heightened risks from poverty, health, conflict, limitation in rights, and environmental degradation. Given the persistence of human security issues in the Global South, mitigating their impact requires enhanced data collection systems, more potent intersectional approaches, and coordinated multi-sectoral efforts to develop sustainable, long-term solutions.
Title: Unveiling the human security crisis in the Global South: a scoping review

Abstract: In many African nations, where the labour force continues to grow annually, employment creation remains a significant challenge. Agriculture remains the largest source of employment across the continent; however, its potential is constrained by several factors, notably limited access to credit owing to low levels of financial inclusion. The COVID-19 pandemic has further disrupted both financial and employment opportunities. In this context, the rapid advancement of information and communication technology (ICT) presents a promising avenue for improving access to financial services through digital platforms, particularly for underserved populations. This, in turn, can facilitate access to credit and support job creation. This study examines the role of digital financial inclusion (DFI) in generating agricultural employment in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic. Using panel data from 26 SSA countries spanning the years 2014 to 2021, the analysis employs the System Generalized Method of Moments (SGMM) approach. The findings indicate that both digital access and usage significantly enhance employment in the agricultural sector. Moreover, the DFI is emerging as a critical driver of job creation in agriculture. Based on these results, this study recommends that governments and policymakers focus on expanding digital infrastructure in rural areas, developing inclusive digital payment ecosystems, promoting digital agricultural marketplaces, and investing in digital skills and financial literacy. Strengthening data protection frameworks is also essential to safeguard personal information and prevent financial crimes.
Title: Addressing jobs generation in a post-crisis context: the effect of digital financial inclusion on agricultural jobs in Sub-Saharan Africa

Abstract: Women living in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) confronts with disproportionately high burden of intimate partner violence (IPV), a global public health concern, which significantly impacts millions of women around the world. Despite such importance, there is very limited literature capturing the trends and revealing the patterns of womens attitudinal acceptance of wife-beating, especially in the context of Bangladesh. This study investigates the socio-demographic factors correlated with the attitudinal acceptance of IPV and examines the trends and patterns persisting among women in Bangladesh using nationally representative data from the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) of 2011, 2014 and 2017-18, which are analyzed using the descriptive statistics and multivariate logistic regression model. The findings reveal a noticeable decline in attitudinal acceptance of wife-beating across the survey years though it varies in rural-urban contexts. More specifically, rural women experience 13.95% points decline in the prevalence of wife-beating (2011: 37.09%, 2017-18: 23.14%) while it declines by 10.68% points among the urban women (2011: 29.19%, 2017-18: 18.51%). Findings from multivariate regression model reveal that women in higher wealth index quintile show significantly lower acceptance of wife-beating compared to those from lower wealth index quintile, implying a negative association between them. Similar findings are also evident in case of educational qualification of women and their husband, i.e., the higher the level of their education, the lower the level of justifying wife-beating. The odds of attitudinal acceptance of wife-beating are higher among rural women than their urban counterparts, implying a significant womens empowerment gap regarding their residential areas. Therefore, policies prioritizing education for rural women would help reduce the prevailing attitudes towards wife-beating in Bangladesh. It is also necessary to disseminate womens rights and establish social justice through increased access to media and information with a view to reducing the attitudinal acceptance of wife-beating in Bangladesh.
Title: Trends and patterns in womens attitude towards wife-beating in Bangladesh: insights from three waves nationally representative survey

Abstract: Pakistans political uncertainty seriously affects national governance, societal cohesion, and regional stability. Although previous studies have examined political instability in Pakistan, there is a lack of comprehensive analysis that includes socio-political and economic aspects. This research addresses that knowledge gap by studying political instability and how cultural and economic values affect governance. The study utilized mixed approaches. The qualitative component included 55 in-depth interviews with academic leaders, local politicians, media communication experts, and sector professionals. The qualitative data suggest that socioeconomic disparity, political corruption, and regional conflicts cause instability. Participants stressed open governance, inclusive economic changes, and regional communication to calm the political environment. The structured surveys 675 respondents comprised university professors, undergraduate and graduate scholars, and the general public. The results show that economic hardship, governance issues, and societal dissatisfaction contribute to political instability. Culture amplifies societal discontent, and the national economic image mediates corruption and instability. The study is crucial for policymakers to promote political stability via equitable economic policies, community involvement, and institutional improvements. Based on Pakistans data, the studys findings have substantial implications for other emerging nations with governance challenges. However, the datas national emphasis and non-probability sample may restrict generalizability.
Title: Analyzing financial drivers of perceived political stability in Pakistan: the role of corruption, social unrest, and cross-border tensions

Abstract: Tourism development in small lakes has gradually been recognized, yet the institutional structures and arrangements for initiating and establishing tourism still need to be overcome. This requires exploring the necessary but rudimentary components of tourism in small lakes by introducing and embracing the Lake Tourism core concept. Thus, this paper argues that Lake Tourism is the essential foundation needed in instituting small lake factors, but it is often absent or incomplete, making it challenging to commence, develop, and expand tourism. Lake Tourism is about cataloging and understanding the intrinsic constituents of tourism development in small lakes, specifically, the lakes center, accessibility, facilities, and accommodations. The central theme contributes to the literature by clarifying the meaning of the Lake Tourism concept and its related components concerning small lakes. It also incorporates comprehending and representing the tourism development and small lakes, especially in introducing and establishing Lake Tourism, while providing the groundwork for future empirical research and studies.
Title: Lake tourism concept and its components: leveraging experience from small lakes in the Philippines

Abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has ignited diverse sociotechnical imaginaries, encompassing both utopian visions of technological advancement and dystopian fears of societal disruption. These imaginaries, constructed by various societal actors, significantly influence public perception and policy-making regarding AI. This study aims to explore and analyze the dominant narratives surrounding AI in Italy, particularly those related to ChatGPT tool. By examining these narratives, the research seeks to uncover the underlying expectations and concerns that shape public engagement with AI technologies. The study uses data collected from social media platforms, particularly Facebook, to capture public discourse on AI. Semantic network analysis and text mining techniques are applied to a dataset of over 3000 Facebook posts discussing ChatGPT and AI extracted by API scraping techniques. The analysis reveals a complex landscape of AI-related discourse, characterized by both utopian and dystopian narratives. Utopian narratives emphasize AIs potential to enhance human capabilities, foster innovation, and address global challenges. Conversely, dystopian narratives highlight concerns about privacy, security, job displacement, and the potential exacerbation of social inequalities. The study underscores the importance of inclusive and participatory approaches to AI governance. Understanding and addressing the diverse narratives that shape public perception is crucial for policymakers to navigate the challenges and opportunities presented by AI.
Title: Imagining AI: exploring narratives and sociotechnical imaginaries between utopias and dystopias

Abstract: Farmers satisfaction with the advisory services provided by agricultural input dealers plays a crucial role in determining the dealers effectiveness as para-extension workers. This study aims to assess the level of farmers satisfaction with these advisory services in the rainfed regions of Andhra Pradesh. The research was conducted during JanuaryFebruary 2024 in the Anantapur and Kurnool districts, which are characterized by extensive rainfed agricultural practices. A total of 120 farmers, selected through a simple random sampling method, participated in the study. A descriptive research design was adopted, and analytical tools such as Importance-Performance Analysis (IPA) and the Customer Satisfaction Index (CSI) were employed to evaluate the data. The findings revealed a moderate level of satisfaction, with a CSI score of 56.30%. Attributes such as fair pricing, yield improvement, trustworthiness, consistency, cost-effectiveness, effectiveness of recommendations, knowledge level, accuracy of information, and problem-solving skills were identified as critical yet underperforming areas that require improvement. Conversely, input dealers performed well in attributes like clarity and understanding, interaction quality, customization, relevance of advice, alignment of inputs with advice, ease of access, and timeliness, which positively influenced farmers satisfaction. The study highlights the need for targeted improvements in key advisory attributes to enhance the overall effectiveness and credibility of input dealers in delivering agricultural support services.
Title: Importance performance analysis to assess farmers satisfaction on advisory services provided by input dealers in rainfed region of Andhra Pradesh

Abstract: The study investigates the impact of digital capital on both consumption poverty and multidimensional poverty in Bangladesh by using the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) 2016. Employing the Propensity Score Matching (PSM) method for impact evaluation, the study examines the impact of digital capital on poverty reduction in Bangladesh, including rural and urban settings. The findings show that access to digital capital reduces lower and upper-consumption poverty by about 57% and about 911%, respectively, depending on the different matching methods. Similarly, the lower multidimensional poverty is reduced by about 23% across different matching specifications. Disaggregate-level findings present a much stronger poverty-reduction impact in rural areas compared to urban areas. For instance, lower-income poverty is reduced by about 911% in rural areas, compared to 24% in urban areas. The most substantial poverty-reduction effect is observed in the upper consumption group, which decreases by about 1317% for the rural areas and by about 6% for the urban areas. Concerning multidimensional poverty, about 57% and 110% poverty reductions are observed for the lower and upper categories, respectively. However, digital capital appears ineffective in reducing multidimensional poverty for urban people at both lower and upper levels. The obtained findings underscore the importance of expanding equitable access to digital capital as a strategic policy priority to combat poverty in Bangladesh effectively.
Title: Impact of access to digital capital on poverty reduction in Bangladesh

Abstract: With the gradual depletion of land-based resources, the sustainable use of ocean and marine resources is gaining global attention, particularly in coastal and developing nations like Bangladesh. This paper examines the importance of blue economy sectors in supporting Bangladeshs sustainable economic growth and explores how rising geostrategic competition among major powers in the Bay of Bengal region may pose challenges to the development of Bangladeshs blue economy. This paper argues that Bangladesh can achieve sustainable economic growth by exploring and utilizing the blue economy sectors. It also argues that Bangladesh must maintain balanced cooperation with its development partners involved in the Bay of Bengal region to develop its blue economy. This study applies a narrative review method to synthesize existing literature on Bangladeshs blue economy potential and geostrategic competition in the Bay of Bengal. Findings suggest that while Bangladeshs blue economy offers enormous development potential, navigating the geostrategic competition in the Bay of Bengal region through balanced cooperation with development partners will be crucial for its successful implementation.
Title: The blue economy of Bangladesh: a development opportunity amid geostrategic competition in the Bay of Bengal region

Abstract: For decades, archaeological work on the Swahili civilization has concentrated mainly on the exploration of economic and political dynamics. This work moves further and explores how gender roles were formed, maintained, negotiated, and renegotiated through time and space in Gede city. The study employed several methods of data collection, namely, archival research, survey, the re-examination of collected materials, and the excavation of the Gede archaeological site. Since this study aimed to examine gender roles across different social classes, the areas excavated were roughly categorized as belonging to elite, middle-class, and lower-class structures. Key findings show that gender identities differed considerably across classes at the Gede archaeological site. This differentiation corresponded with the commercialization of Gede households, especially in elite areas where the high class hosted international traders. Conversely, in middle-class houses, women concentrated on running light industries aimed at supplying goods to the urban community. Thus, women were able to afford exotic goods as were their elite counterparts. Finally, the gender roles of the lower class entailed subsistence-gendered roles with little participation in Gede formal commerce. Interestingly, gender roles in Gede were dynamic in nature and responded to cultural diffusion, the spread of Islam, the intensification of trade, the diversification of subsistence patterns, and urbanization. Therefore, these findings demonstrate the centrality of gender in the reconstruction of social lives during the Swahili civilization.
Title: Social identities in built environments? Interrogating gendered categories in Gede city during the Swahili civilization

Abstract: This study explored the perceived benefits and challenges of using L2-French as the mandatory medium of instruction for scientific subjects in Moroccan secondary education, along with the role of translanguaging in addressing students learning difficulties. L2-French medium instruction (FMI) is part of the Language Alternation (LA) policy, which involves teaching natural sciences, physics, and mathematics in foreign languages while using Standard Arabic, the official language, for other subjects. The quantitative data presented in this paper are part of a comprehensive mixed-methods study that examined the perspectives of teachers, students, and administrators, providing valuable insights into this new educational experience within the Moroccan context. Analyses were conducted using SPSS software, employing descriptive statistics and non-parametric inferential tests. The findings indicated that students from disadvantaged backgrounds in rural and public schools, who struggle with their French proficiency, hold a more negative outlook on their language and conceptual development in this new environment compared to their counterparts in urban and private schools. Additionally, the evidence suggests that translanguaging can serve as a supportive strategy for students with low French proficiency, helping to alleviate the challenges associated with the new policy. This study offers implications for leveraging the new policy and mitigating students difficulties.
Title: L2-French-medium instruction (FMI) in Moroccan secondary education: benefits, challenges, and the role of translanguaging

Abstract: Living alone is both a choice and a compulsion among the elderly in India as the country is undergoing demographic and social transitions. An interplay of economic, health, and social factors affect their living arrangements and, hence, life satisfaction. The present study tries to analyse the factors affecting the psychosocial wellbeing (i.e. life satisfaction) of the elderly through the mediation of living arrangements. The study used data on the elderly population (60 years and above) from the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI), wave 1 (201718). Life satisfaction and satisfaction with living arrangement were measured to determine the factors affecting life satisfaction while focussing upon the living alone arrangement. The study used descriptive statistics and summary measures for the analysis. Social, economic, and health indices were used to measure the composite effect on living arrangement and satisfaction through the path analysis. It was found that the prevalence of living alone (5%) was the highest among elderly females, elderly who were not currently married, those with a low level of education, and those suffering from depression. Social and economic performance, measured through composite indices, was found to be low among the elderly living alone in comparison to the others. The path analysis suggested that economic status influenced the living arrangement of the elderly to a great extent; however, satisfaction with living arrangement was also determined by the social status of the elderly.
