The outcome of life satisfaction goes beyond the simple choice of living arrangement rather satisfaction is derived from living arrangements. The elderly living alone should be given economic and social security to promote healthy aging and optimum wellbeing.
Title: Life satisfaction and psychosocial wellbeing among elderly living alone in India

Abstract: Developing countries (Nigeria among others) are in severe socioeconomic and political conundrums. These challenges had made the countries to lag behind among the comity of nations. Before the outbreak of COVID-19 in the late 2019 and its pandemic status in early 2020, Nigerias socioeconomic and political index such as inflation rate, poverty level, unemployment level, misery ranking, insecurity, communal violence and other forms of insecurity are on the high side. The outbreak of COVID-19 compounded the problems to the extent of raising the levels of poverty, misery and insecurity in the country. The objective of this study is to proffer answers to how developing countries (Nigeria) can mitigate the effects of the ravaging COVID-19 pandemic on the socioeconomic and political landscape of the country. Cognitive interpretive research method is utilised to obtain and analyse data. Secondary data from World Bank are utilised. Poverty cycle is utilised as an intervention amidst COVID-19 pandemic era. Poverty and structural functionalism theory is used to explain the political economy effects of COVID-19 pandemic. The paper finds and concluded that the political economy effect of COVID-19 will linger for a long time in Nigeria because the underlining challenges inherent in the political system before COVID-19 advents had not been resolved. To mitigate this, poverty cycle must be broken as an immediate intervention.
Title: Poverty cycle and post COVID-19 interventions in Nigeria: a political economy perspective

Abstract: Despite the growing consensus that the emotional intelligence of service employees influences customer satisfaction and trust, it remains unclear whether the emotional intelligence of university lecturers affects students satisfaction, trust in lecturers, and overall satisfaction with universities. This study examines the relationship between the dimensions of emotional intelligence and students satisfaction with lecturers, trust of lecturers, and satisfaction with university. Data was collected from 164 lecturers and 164 students in two universities in Ghana. Structural equation modelling was used to analyse the data. The results showed self-emotional appraisal, regulation of emotion, and others emotional appraisal influence students satisfaction with lecturer, and trust of lecturer. However, the use of emotion did not predict the satisfaction with lecturer, and trust in lecturer. The study found that the dimensions of emotional intelligence do not predict satisfaction with higher education institution. On the other hand, satisfaction with university and trust in lecturer are predictors of satisfaction with university. Various implications emerge from the findings. They include (a) emotional intelligence must become an integral part of the training and development of university employees to have a healthy and positive relationships with students, (b) training of university employees must focus on all the aspects of emotional intelligence (c) higher education institutions have the ability to enhance students satisfaction and trust as a result of the emotional intelligence of employees, (d) university employees must be conscious of and exhibit emotional intelligence in their interactions with students, (e) higher education institutions can market their institutions using the emotional intelligence capabilities of employees.
Title: Emotional intelligence, student trust and student satisfaction in higher education institutions

Abstract: This study explores the infrastructural and financial challenges confronting higher education institutions in Ghana and identifies strategies for building resilience within the sector. Through a systematic review of literature and relevant secondary data, the study highlights the pervasive issues of inadequate physical and technological infrastructure, exacerbated by growing student populations and insufficient financial resources. Resilience theory was selected for this study because of its dynamic, process-oriented framework, which closely aligns with the studys emphasis on long-term sustainability and capacity building. Unlike Resource Dependence Theory and Institutional Theory, which offer more static perspectives, resilience theory captures the adaptive and evolving responses institutions employ when confronted with internal and external disruptions. A central tenet of resilience in this context is the ability of universities to diversify their resources and effectively adjust to shifting circumstances. Key findings reveal that public universities face delayed government subventions, heavy dependence on tuition fees, and limited financial autonomy, which collectively hinder their operational efficiency and quality of education. The analysis further emphasizes the technological infrastructure gap, especially exposed during the COVID-19 pandemic, which constrained effective online learning. In response, resilience strategies such as Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs), internally generated funds, and revenue diversification have been identified as viable solutions. These strategies underscore the need for innovative financial models, collaborative partnerships, and institutional reforms to sustain higher education amidst resource constraints. The study advocates for proactive policy frameworks and capacity building to ensure the long-term sustainability and competitiveness of Ghanaian higher education institutions.
Title: Building resilience in higher education by addressing infrastructure and financial resource challenges in Ghana

Abstract: This study explored the interaction between formal social intervention programmes and traditional support networks in the Volta Region of Ghana. It aimed to understand whether the introduction of formal programmes has augmented or diminished the provision of informal support to vulnerable populations. Primary data were collected from three districts in the Volta Region using semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions. A total of 63 participants, including beneficiaries and non-beneficiaries of formal protection programmes, district authorities, community and religious leaders, and media representatives, contributed to the data. This study reveals that formal social protection initiatives have neither undermined nor actively reinforced traditional support systems. National and local leaders have made no effort to integrate formal and informal support systems, leading them to function independently. This lack of coordination limits the potential of collaboration to address the needs of vulnerable populations. Policymakers and implementers should: (i) initiate and sustain dialogue as a useful first step for integrating traditional support structures into formal social interventions, (ii) incorporate relevant elements of traditional support into formal programmes, and (iii) lend credibility to such integration through legal and policy recognition. This study offers a unique contribution to the understanding of the coexistence of formal and traditional social protection systems in Ghana. It highlights missed opportunities for collaboration between these systems and proposes a coordinated model that departs from isolated social protection approaches in the existing literature.
Title: Enhancing social protection: examining the interaction between formal programs and traditional support systems in the Volta Region of Ghana

Abstract: This paper explores methodological issues concerning the operationalization of ethnicity in the field of education. The sole criterion of citizenship often applied in official educational statistics may exclude naturalized students with foreign and/or immigrant origins from the non-national category. The challenge of collecting reliable statistics on ethnic origins has become crucial in most Western European countries in recent years, as the quantification of this phenomenon is a fundamental starting point for the implementation of policies aimed at contrasting ethnic inequality and discrimination. Resorting to the 2011 Italian general population census, a multi-dimensional typology combining students and parents countries of birth, citizenship at census and citizenship at birth has been developed. Although the detection of ethnic origins should not be problematic in a country where the acquisition of citizenship is based on the right of blood, results reveal that official statistics classify almost 1 million students (9.35%) with foreign- and/or immigrant-origins as nationals. Moreover, an in-depth exploration of the origin country allows one to discern between native-born descendants of non-nationals born abroad and native-born descendants of Italian emigrants born abroad. This multi-dimensional typology may be a useful tool for obtaining more reliable data and implementing more effective policies to address educational inequalities.
Title: Operationalizing ethnic origins: a multi-dimensional typology

Abstract: The Sustainable Development Goals consist of 17 interconnected global objectives aimed at creating a better and more sustainable future for everyone. This paper examines the factors that shape citizens visions of an ideal society across twelve European countries. Understanding that the idea of an ideal society is both aspirational and context-dependent, the study utilises the Sustainable Livelihoods Approach, Collaborative Planning Theory, and Human Ecology Theory to interpret the priorities of citizens. The research analyses various factors, including poverty, safety and security, religious values, immigration policies, longevity, freedom, military strength, inequality, education quality, economic prosperity, birth rates, trust, human rights, democracy, and social connections. Using data from the CROss-National Online Survey 2 (CRONOS-2), the study applies factor analysis to identify correlation patterns among these variables. The results suggest that social well-being and social life have a more significant impact on shaping citizens visions of an ideal society than traditional values and security concerns. The research findings suggest that social well-being plays a crucial role in shaping these ideal visions of society. It highlights the importance of implementing policies that aim to improve education, alleviate poverty, safeguard human rights, and foster trust. These results emphasise the crucial role of normative frameworks in promoting sustainable development and are closely aligned with various key Sustainable Development Goals.
Title: Critical factors in reaching an ideal society

Abstract: This paper examines the preferences of former female civil servants in Afghanistan toward the countrys future under Taliban rule. After the Talibans takeover in August 2021, womens roles in government significantly declined, and many were forced to leave their jobs or even the country. Surprisingly, however, our earlier survey of former female civil servants found that about half of the respondents expressed a willingness to work for the government again due to economic difficulties. Building upon this unexpected finding, we conducted a follow-up survey involving a conjoint experiment with 156 former female civil servants. The survey assessed how they balance competing priorities, such as job availability, womens rights, corruption, and the regime. Major findings include: (1) all four factors influenced respondents preferences; (2) the regime was the most important factor, with respondents showing preferences against the current regime; and (3) economic opportunities were as important as womens rights. These results underscore the importance of economic conditions and also suggest that the situation regarding women and female civil servants can be more complex than how outsiders might see the current state of Afghanistan.
Title: Assessing the relative importance of job opportunities: a conjoint experiment of former civil servants in Afghanistan

Abstract: Mock interviews play a crucial part in improving employability, particularly by improving effective communicationa fundamental skill in job interviews. While technical knowledge is still essential, the ability to explain ideas effectively and confidently is also critical, especially for undergraduate students from the countryside who may have had little experience to formal interview settings. As the competition for placements intensifies, mock interviews provide a valuable opportunity for students to practice, receive feedback, and build the confidence needed to succeed in real-world interviews. This study assessed student performance in mock interviews by evaluating verbal and non-verbal communication, technical skills, and overall interview readiness. Existing datasets, rubrics, and evaluation techniques used in mock interview assessments were analyzed, revealing their limitations in providing a holistic evaluation. To address these gaps, a new dataset was developed, incorporating verbal, non-verbal, technical, and non-technical skills. Features were extracted from interview videos, and regression models, including Random Forest Regressor, Support Vector Regressor, and Ridge Regressor, were applied to predict overall student performance. The results demonstrated that the newly developed dataset provided a more comprehensive assessment than existing benchmark datasets. Among the applied models, Random Forest Regressor exhibited the highest predictive capability. These findings underscored the importance of integrating diverse assessment criteria for more accurate interview evaluations. Future work should refine assessment criteria and explore advanced machine learning techniques to enhance prediction accuracy and feedback effectiveness.
Title: Investigating job interview performance with a cutting-edge dataset of undergraduate students

Abstract: Mangroves are amongst the most efficient carbon-sequestering ecosystems, andS. apetalais one of the key species which is planted along the coastal belt in Bangladesh. However, silvicultural operations like thinning on the carbon stock of this planted species is still inconclusive. Here, several silvicultural approaches (with or without thinning and with or without recruitment) was conducted to compare the development of planted forests in terms of forest management. Also, an individual-based model (e.g., KiWi model) has been created to evaluate demographic processes in coastal mangrove forests using abiotic environmental parameters. The findings demonstrate that 3.5m radius thinning produces the highest aboveground carbon stocks in inS. apetalaplantations in the study area. In Bangladesh coastal plantations, the 2.5m and 3.0m thinning radius are ideal because they include an adequate number of trees while producing as much aboveground carbon as the 3.5m thinning radius. This experiment strongly demonstrates that the KiWi model can simulate genuine dynamic growth patterns and that thinning has an influence on carbon stock. Simulation experiments tailored to the study sites configurations gave a forecast of future stand development, which is critical for mangrove forest management and policy implementation.
Title: Effect of thinning on carbon stocks inSonneratia apetalaBuch. -Ham plantations: a simulation study in Bangladesh

Abstract: Extant literature on the association between benevolent sexism and womens identity reconfiguration in the context oflobolaor bride price valuations has continued to attract fervent interest among scholars and practitioners in Africa in general and Zimbabwe in particular. Although there has not been consensus on both the socio-cultural and economic constructs of the nature and significance oflobola, the study on which this paper is based extends previous scholarly works particularly by Chisango et al. (2022) and Vengesayi (2018) in terms of howlobola(i.e. bride price) is being determined and practised in modern African cultures. The study acknowledges that apart from the predicted association between benevolent sexism and bride price, there was also a link between perceptions of a womans morality and physical attractiveness (operationalised asmorality-physical attractiveness), and scale oflobolapricing. The hypotheses were tested with a Zimbabwean sample (n=405; mean age=42.20,SD=11.15). Results provided support for the hypotheses, with the effect of main importance being that benevolent sexism mediated the relationship betweenmorality-physical attractivenessandlobolapricing. Results are further discussed in line with ambivalent sexism theory and their wider implications. The study conclusion reinforces other studies that found that valuation oflobolawas not only driven by economic imperatives but could be a form of heteronormative discourse signalling symbolic violence that undermines gender equality and ultimately, womens emancipation.
Title: Benevolent sexist valuation oflobolain contemporary Zimbabwe

Abstract: Over the past two decades, translanguaging has increasingly garnered the attention and interest of scholars, frequently serving as a theoretical or practical framework. This study utilizes bibliometric analysis to create a comprehensive knowledge map of social justice research from a translanguaging perspective, drawing on 20 years of data from the Web of Science (WoS) database. The analysis encompasses articles published between 2004 and 2023 to illustrate the status of social justice research through a translanguaging lens, identify key research topics, and suggest future research directions. By using the keywords translanguaging and social justice and filtering for articles and early access publications, 475 articles were retrieved. The findings, derived from production, content, and citation analysis using a bibliometric tool, highlight three key points: first, research in this area demonstrates notable growth and potential, with increasing contributions from diverse authors, institutions, and countries. Second, central themes such as language, language policy, and multilingualism underscore the fields multifaceted nature, while multimodality emerges as a key topic for future exploration. Third, the study highlights macro, meso, and micro levels of engagement. At the macro level, policymakers can enhance their assessment of the effectiveness of institutions, universities, and scholars in promoting social justice through translanguaging research. At the meso level, schools and teachers should harness students linguistic potential and foster equitable practices. At the micro level, students are encouraged to utilize diverse resources and challenge monolingual norms. This study emphasizes the potential of translanguaging research to advance social justice in multilingual education.
Title: Translanguaging towards social justice: a bibliometric review of research (20042023)

Abstract: This study explores the conflicting factions that have emerged in the ideological debate surrounding the issue of women driving in Saudi Arabia: the pro- and anti-driving campaigns. The pro-driving faction argues for womens autonomy and societal progress, while the opposition primarily fears social destabilization, health consequences, and religious disapproval. These factions engage in discourse onX(formerly Twitter), a platform chosen for its wide-reaching influence and real-time exchange of ideas. Unlike previous research that primarily examined the debates written characteristics, this study includes visual content, using critical discourse analysis to analyze posts textual and visual elements. Van Dijks (2004) framework for analyzing ideological discourse and Faircloughs (1992b) concept of intertextuality are applied to examine the images attached to a sample of tweets. The findings reveal that images not only complement the written discourse but also serve as a tool for reinforcing or undermining arguments. The pro-driving faction uses images to mock religious claims against women driving and to memorialize early activists struggles, while the opposing faction employs images to emphasize the failure of MBCs June 15 poll and assert their ideological position. The analysis underscores the importance of considering both textual and visual elements in understanding social and political debates. This study contributes to the growing literature on digital discourse and multimodality, demonstrating how images and text co-construct and challenge societal ideologies. The implications suggest that a comprehensive understanding of discourse requires an awareness of the social and cultural contexts shaping the production and interpretation of visual and written content.
Title: Imagery and debate: a critical discourse analysis of women driving in Saudi Arabia pre-ban lift

Abstract: The role of urban fruit trees in enhancing environmental sustainability, socio-economic resilience, and global food security has garnered growing global attention. However, their potential in promoting sustainable development, particularly within informal settlements, remains under-recognized. This study investigates local preferences and perceptions regarding the integration of fruit trees into urban landscapes in informal settlements in Kumasi, Ghana, to inform urban planning and sustainability strategies. Using Sawaba, one of the major informal settlements as a case study, the study addresses two key questions: how are fruit trees perceived in informal settlement, and what are the landscape preferences of residents for sustainability? The study employs a mixed-method approach including household surveys, interviews with 3 experts including the Head of the Department of Parks and Gardens, the Physical Planner from Asokore Mampong Municipality, and the Assembly Member of Sawaba, and scenario analysis (drawings of landscapes with distinct tree placements as graphical scenarios). The study found that the most identified fruit tree species were mango (25.9%), coconut (25.4%), and orange (22.8%). Respondents cited income generation (25.3%) and employment opportunities (22.3%) as the leading socio-economic benefits, environmental benefits included improved air quality (15.7%), provision of shade (15.5%), and beautification of the community (12.4%). Scenario analysis showed that the most preferred landscape scenario was trees planted in front of houses (56%), followed by trees planted throughout the area (20%), trees only at the back (13%), and no trees (11%). This study maintains that while recognizing these diverse landscape preferences, it is essential that city authorities undertake community sensitization campaigns on planting and protecting indigenous fruit tree species to enhance environmental and socio-economic outcomes in informal settlements.
Title: The integration of fruit trees into urban landscapes: insights from informal settlements in Kumasi

Abstract: E-learning platforms have evolved as a highly successful means of learning, with recommender systems functioning as useful tools for assisting users in selecting the most appropriate courses. MOOCs (Massive Open Online Resources) have drifted the traditional teaching-learning approach from chalk-duster to the digital platform. MOOCs (Massive Open Online Resources) boosts the personalized learning by customize learning and suggesting e-content depending on the users preferences, interests, and search history. The purpose of this study is to discover and predict the parameters influencing the success of MOOCs (Massive Open Online Resources). These parameters depict the relationship between the factors stating the effectiveness of MOOCs (Massive Open Online Resources) known as EMOOCs. In this paper, the objective of the research objective is to propose the recommender model predicting the performance metrics of the study. To achieve the research objectives the following tasks are performed: a) Exploring the factors influencing the MOOCs (Massive Open Online Resources) b) By evaluating RMSE and MSE values to investigate the relationship between the parameters affecting the effectiveness of MOOCs (EMOOCs) c) To predict the performance metrics various Machine Learning Algorithms are implemented. d) Furthermore, the performance metrics values recommend the best algorithm for building the Recommender model e) Finally, to test and validate the results of the models- Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) is formulated using the Partial Least Squares (PLS) Smart-PLS 4 Software.
Title: Recommender system for predicting MOOCs effectiveness in technical courses

Abstract: In recent years, the quality of democracy in Mexico has declined gradually but steadily. Several indices agree that democracy has been particularly affected by the arrival of Andrs Manuel Lpez Obrador to the Executive Branch in 2018, labelled by the literature as a populist leader. By reviewing Lpez Obradors governmental actions, this article will study the relationship between the Presidents populist attitudes and the quality of democracy in Mexico. The methodology employs a qualitative approach with a descriptive scope, providing a thorough discussion of the populist administration and democratic backsliding in the Mexican case. Furthermore, the analysis ofTeam Populismsholistic grading of Lpez Obradors actions and discourses, as well as democratic indices to demonstrate the democratic backlash, has been mostly evident during AMLOs administration. The primary objective is to examine how the populist administration behaved in office, thereby undermining Mexican democracy. This article will focus on the Governments functioning and, specifically, the former Presidents leadership, tendencies, and decisions that have influenced Mexicos future.
Title: Populist leadership and democratic backlash. a study of AMLOs presidency in Mexico

Abstract: Various public entities across different developing countries are plagued by poor service delivery, which predominantly stems from poor governance. Innumerable citizens are experiencing inadequate access to essential housing services. Despite the growing literature on good governance and service delivery, empirical studies on citizens lived experiences of the subject are still unavailable, particularly in South Africa. Thus, this study strives to empirically fill the gap by exploring the citizens lived experiences of the effects of good governance practices on housing service delivery. The study adopted a qualitative research approach and data was solicited from traditional leaders at four local municipalities in South Africa using semi-structured interviews to accomplish the studys objectives. Qualitative usable data from 14 participants were thematically analysed. The study revealed that citizens lived experiences confirm the positive influence good governance practices have on service delivery. The results revealed that adherence to governance principles such as transparency and accountability is fundamental to ensuring that governance practices translate into tangible improvements in service delivery. The practical implication of the study is that management must ensure that all municipality officials and councillors abide by the principles of good governance daily. Another key implication of these findings is that municipalities should invest in the training and development of municipal staff about transparency practices, which is necessary to improve service delivery.
Title: Exploring the lived experiences of citizens on the effects of good governance practices on housing service delivery: a case study of four municipalities in South Africa

Abstract: This study underscores the critical role of local government autonomy (LGA) in Nigeria as a catalyst for achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) at the grassroots governance level. It examines governance inefficiencies and explores how digital tools, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), can enhance transparency, accountability, and service delivery. Utilizing a systematic literature review (SLR) and in-depth interviews with 25 stakeholdersincluding policymakers and local government officialsthe research identifies key barriers such as constitutional ambiguities, state dominance, weak financial independence, corruption, and inadequate infrastructure. These challenges directly limit local governance and impede progress toward key SDG targets: SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), and SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions). Enhancing local autonomy through digital tools like AI, the study proposes a pathway to improve governance efficiency and accountability, which are essential for grassroots development. Reliance on dwindling federally allocated revenues exacerbates financial constraints, hindering the implementation of poverty reduction programs. Integrating AI-driven governance models (AI-DGMs) and digital tax collection can offer innovative solutions, supporting SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure) by facilitating better resource allocation, enhancing transparency, and reducing corruption. These factors are vital for fostering trust in governmental institutions. The findings contribute to the discourse on governance in Nigeria and present a conceptual framework that integrates policy reforms and technology solutions, essential for realizing the SDGs. Addressing structural challenges through constitutional reforms and investments in digital infrastructure will be crucial for promoting effective decentralization and enhancing local responsiveness to development goals.
Title: From control to collaboration: stakeholder perspectives on rethinking local governance and state guardianship through the prism of digital technology for sustainable grassroots transformation

Abstract: The dataset generated by the coding of the judicial material analysed during the current study cannot be publicly available following the Italian law, due to procedural and privacy rules, since it contains also taped conversations with sensitive information on individuals not prosecuted nor convicted. Excerpts with anonymised data could be made available on reasonable request.
Title: Symbols and reputation in a corruption network: the Mondo Di mezzo (Middle-earth) operation in Rome

Abstract: There is a widespread belief that mathematics is the most value-free of all school subjects among stakeholders in mathematics education, especially teachers. However, some mathematics educators and researchers are convinced that mathematics is culture-embedded and, therefore, value-driven. This present study aimed at exploring senior high school (SHS) mathematics teachers teaching practices of mathematical values in a municipality in Ghana. In the quest to achieve the purpose of this study, we employed explanatory sequential mixed methods. In the quantitative study, a census was employed to include all 53 SHS mathematics teachers within the Tano South Municipality. For the qualitative phase, purposive sampling was used to select six SHS mathematics teachers recruited to complete the questionnaires in the quantitative phase to participate in interviews. The quantitative data were analyzed using both descriptive statistics (percentage, frequency, mean, and standard deviations) and inferential statistics (one-way between-groups analysis of variance [ANOVA]). The qualitative data also was analyzed using a thematic analysis. From the studys findings, it was concluded that SHS mathematics teachers often practiced the mathematical values ofobjectism,control,progress, andopenness. In contrast, other mathematical values, such asrationalismandmystery, were sometimes practiced. The mathematical values teaching practice among SHS mathematics teachers who teach at Basic 10, 11, and 12 was statistically significantly different. It is, therefore, recommended, among others, that teacher education institutions review their mathematics programs to promote values and valuing in mathematics education among pre-service mathematics teachers.
Title: From professing to doing: mathematical values practices of high school mathematics teachers

Abstract: While international literature indicates that students first language constitutes a great advantage in their learning, the system of education in Morocco is still monolingual and promotes the use of a single medium of instruction. This study examined the factors behind freshmens preference for a certain medium of instruction in learning science subjects and the obstacles they face with exclusive reliance on one medium. It employed a mixed-methods research design. 104 freshmen from three departments at the Faculty of Science were surveyed through a questionnaire and 24 of them were randomly selected to participate in semi-structured interviews. Correlation tests were used to examine the quantitative data, and thematic analysis was utilized to analyze the qualitative data. Findings indicated that a variety of factors, including students perception of the role their first language plays in facilitating the learning process, their language proficiency, and their use of different languages in other spheres of daily life accounted for their preference for a particular medium of instruction. Our findings suggest that adopting a multilingual approach to education that recognizes all languages as valuable resources for learning and embraces students multilingualism through the use of their first language alongside the medium of instruction would create an inclusive and enriched learning environment that promotes effective learning and cognitive development.
Title: Beyond monolingualism: the benefits of translanguaging in science education

Abstract: Peoples perceptions, attitudes, and socioeconomic factors influence their adaptation strategies, which are critical to addressing the impacts of climate change in order to maintain a sustainable environment and social stability. This research aimed to explore how people perceive climate change and what factors influence farmers adaptation measures in response to the effects of a changing climate in a coastal district of southern Bangladesh. This research used a mixed method approach to examine how people understand climate change and the determinants behind farmers adaptation efforts. According to the surveys findings, roughly 56% of respondents have very little view of climate change. 85.3% of survey respondents reported that climate change has already endangered their lives. As was to be expected, the Binary Logit model demonstrated that the vast majority of farmers employed new adaptation strategies to address the bad impacts of climate change. The Multinomial Logit (MNL) model, in contrast, showed a positive and significant correlation between the farmers family size, beliefs, knowledge of the reasons for climate change and information channels, and their adaptation strategies, while also revealing the negative impacts of the farmers gender and age on their adaptation strategy choices. Contrarily, the survey revealed the obstacles that farmers faced to the way of taking adaptation strategies, with a lack of money being cited as the most significant of these obstacles. The study concludes by urging policymakers to take a bottom-up approach to crafting adaptation policies in order to better equip farmers to handle the effects of climate change.
Title: Climate change in the coastal zone of Bangladesh: perceptions and determinants of adaptation strategies

Abstract: Ziro valley of Arunachal Pradesh in India is inhabited by the Apatani tribe. The tribe shares a very interdependent and harmonious relationship with the environment. Known for their sustainable ways of living, this tribe believes in protecting nature and has methods to sustain natural resources. They follow a settled pattern of life and are agrarian However, in recent times; it has been observed that there is tremendous pressure on the traditional sustainable land use practices of the valley. Due to the growth and expansion of economic activities increasing areas are put into use like urban, commercial, industrial, and residential. The percentage of urban population in Ziro valley has increased to 15.42% in 2011 from 10.66% in 1991. The conversion of natural areas to cultivable land, commercial logging, construction of houses, and establishment of industries and commercial areas in agricultural land is increasing in rapid phases at Ziro Valley. The growing urbanization and expanding commercial cultivation, industrialization, commercial logging, and expanding settlement are responsible for the land use and land cover change in the Valley. Apart from forest degradation, land conversion into nonagricultural and commercial agricultural uses through increasing urbanization significantly affects the biodiversity and land degradation of the valley. This study analyzed the changing land use and land cover in the Ziro Valley from 2002 to 2023. There is complex conversion among the land covers. The maximum changes are observed in the increase in built-up areas from 2002 to 2023 which is 186.15%. It is observed that the agricultural lands have been converted into non agricultural activities and the lack of interest among the young generation towards traditional livelihood practices and exposure to the modern world. These findings provide decision support for the sustainable policy making and further promote the exploration of causes behind growing land use land cover change in the study area.
Title: LULC changes and driving forces thereof in Ziro Valley, Lower Subansiri District, Arunachal Pradesh

Abstract: The future generation needs to develop an awareness and understanding of harmful ecological threats to make decisions and take actions to mitigate their impact. This study examines the environmental knowledge, awareness, and behavioral aspects of students (specifically of class 10 and 12) in both private and government high schools across all education boards in a representative city (Kolkata) in India. The research work involves the collection of 200 students responses using a 5-point Likert scale questionnaire from high schools belonging to three major accredited boards in Kolkata. The Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS, version 26) software was used to analyze the data. A total of 200 high school students from Class 10 and 12 were selected from 6 CBSE (Central Board of Secondary Education), 6 ICSE (Indian Certificate of Secondary Education) and 8 WB (West Bengal Board of Secondary Education) board accredited high schools using the stratified sampling method. The findings reveal that class 10 and 12 students across all nationally accredited boards have significant moderate positive correlations existing between their environmental awareness and behavioral patterns. Furthermore, class 12 students from the ICSE board scored the highest in terms of environmental behavioral patterns. The intention and attitude of the students were significant positive predictors of students environmental awareness, while the type of education board, intention, and attitude were significant positive predictors of students environmental behavioral patterns. The study accentuates the fact that enhancing environmental education by incorporating more action-based learning into the curriculum for high school students across all boards, while simultaneously supporting these efforts with strong institutional programmes will strengthen students awareness and behavioral patterns in support of environmental sustainability.
Title: An investigation of environmental awareness and behavioral aspects of high school students in Kolkata

Abstract: Informal learning environments are increasingly recognized as transformative spaces for enriching science education through experiential, real-world learning. This study investigated middle school science teachers perceptions and experiences of teaching in informal learning contexts in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. A qualitative multiple-case study design was employed with 14 teachers (Grades 79). Data were collected via semi-structured interviews, written reflective activities, and a focus group discussion, and analyzed thematically using the Curricular Spider Web model as an analytic lens. Findings reveal that while teachers value informal settings for boosting student engagement, curiosity, and understanding, they face significant challenges, notably resource shortages, financial constraints, and curriculum pressures, that hinder effective implementation. Teachers demonstrated resilience and adaptability by improvising with local materials and flexible strategies, though concerns about classroom management and limited training often tempered their use of playful, exploratory learning. The study highlights the need for targeted teacher education and policy support to address systemic barriers and better integrate informal learning opportunities into the curriculum. By utilizing informal environments and supporting teachers, stakeholders can enhance science teaching relevancy and equity, ultimately enriching students science learning experiences.
Title: Science teachers in informal learning contexts in South Africa: perspectives via the curricular spider web model

Abstract: Local governance is a sine qua non for democratic governance. Unfortunately, the distance of government businesses from majority of rural folks in the 1980s did not encourage participatory governance. Through various legal regimes, Ghana tried to overcome this weakness and to encourage participation at the district assemblies. To deepen this, Article 240(1) of the 1992 Republican Constitution of Ghana and the Local Governance Act, 2016 (Act 936) sought to transfer functions, power and means to the grassroots. This paper explores the extent to which the issues of representation, voice, and information-flow are adhered to in four selected districts. Qualitative research approach was used, and analyses done descriptively. The results show that the practice of local governance is enhanced but with lack of capacity support to Assembly members in representing their electorates effectively. The paper concludes that Ghanas local governance system will be more enhanced if the constrained elements are addressed.
Title: Local governance enhancement mechanisms in Ghana: theoretical and practical reflection on representation, voice and information-flow within district assemblies in Ghana

Abstract: Does it pay to get a college degree in music? We answer this question using data from the most recent five years of the American Community Survey, a survey of roughly fifteen million Americans, including over 14,000 professional musicians. We find that the answer differs greatly depending on what one considers to be the alternative to a music degree. Compared to no getting no college degree, music degrees are associated with higher incomes for both musicians and non-musicians. Compared to other college degrees, music degrees are associated with higher incomes for those who work as musicians, but much lower incomes for those who do not. We document a variety of other unusual facts about music as a profession: musicians are 4 times more likely than the average worker to be self-employed, and musicians work 13.7h per week less than the average worker. Musicians who were music majors raise their incomes largely by working more, averaging 5.7 extra hours of work per week compared to non-majors and being 10.2% points more likely to be employed.
Title: Music majors and musician income

Abstract: This paper evaluates the effectiveness of employment policies in Ghana from a gender perspective. Gender disparities turn to exacerbate the problem of youth unemployment in Ghana. Even though several youth employment programs have been implemented in Ghana, their effectiveness from a gender perspective is largely unknown. This study utilizes data from the ARUA Centre of Excellence for Unemployment and Skills Development survey conducted in 2020 and employs descriptive statistical analysis and logistic regression analysis to evaluate the employment policies. The findings show that higher educational attainment among females leads to increased expectations for job quality and career advancement. The results also show that female youth have higher awareness levels in terms of incentives and administration of the programs than their male counterparts. Additionally, the results from the logistic regression analysis show that males have a lower perception of the effectiveness of employment policies in terms of empowerment, capacity building, and job creation than female youth. This paper provides empirical evidence that outlines the gender variation in the perception of the effectiveness of employment policies in Ghana. Thus, it helps in understanding the challenges associated with the NYEA programs in Ghana, filling the gap in the existing literature.
Title: Youth unemployment and the effectiveness of employment policies in Ghana: a gender perspective

Abstract: Climate change impacts like erratic weather patterns, droughts, and floods worsen mental health issues among farmers, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, due to farmers high dependence on agriculture and limited adaptive capacity. While previous studies focused on farmers perceptions and adaptation choices, psychological and social dimensions have received limited attention, constraining effective policy responses and progress toward Sustainable Development Goal 13. This study addresses this gap by examining how psychological and social factors influence coping strategies for climate-induced mental health impacts. A survey of 300 farming households in Ghana was conducted using structured questionnaires, and a multinomial logit model was applied to assess the effects of these factors. Common coping strategies included seeking social support (51.7%), participating in farmers groups (18.7%), and engaging in religious and relaxation activities (11.0%). The model revealed that age increased the likelihood of seeking social support (=0.014,p<0.01) but reduced engagement in stress-reduction activities (=0.005,p<0.01). Farming experience decreased the likelihood of using mental health services (=0.239,p<0.01). Place attachment discouraged social support (=0.178,p<0.01) but promoted stress-reducing strategies ( =0.062,p<0.01). Perceived climate risk increased participation in support groups (=0.175,p<0.1) but lowered mental health service use (=0.224,p<0.01) and information-seeking (=0.491,p<0.01). Cultural beliefs reduced social support (0.668) but increased substance use (=0.159,p<0.01), diversification (=0.305,p<0.01), and climate information-seeking (=0.288,p<0.01). The findings revealed the need for community-based awareness campaigns, stress management interventions, and enhanced social support to build resilience.
Title: Psychosocial factors influencing coping strategies for climate change-related mental health impacts in Northwest Ghana

Abstract: This research sought to investigate the state of psychological safety of academics and its relatedness to experiences of academic freedom and collegiality in Ghanaian universities. The study deployed an enhanced Academic Freedom Scale as well as the Collegiality and Psychological Safety scales to collect data from a sample of 436 respondents surveyed from a cross section of both public and private universities. A regression of the results revealed that academics feel psychologically unsafe, and this perception of insecurity is strongly related to their low-rated experiences of academic freedom and collegiality. This is an indication that the utopian view of the university is a sanctum of learning where the intellect may safely range and speculate is no more. From the relative deprivation theory (RDT) perspective, the discrepancy between an academics lived reality and their a priori assumptions and expectations before or upon entering the university environment may render them disenchanted and insecure, and they may feel defective in their ability to engage with their environment, as they are deprived of a key requisite for the validation of their self-efficacy. Consequently, this may inhibit agentic propensities such as engaging in extra-role behaviors such as proffering proposals and active coworker support and interactivity, which are congruent with collegiality.
Title: Paradise lost- the effect of the erosion of collegiality and academic freedom on psychological safety of academics

Abstract: This paper examines Turkeys strategic engagement in the Horn of Africa and its impact on the Ethiopian security landscape. To this end, this study uses a case study research design and a qualitative research approach that combines primary and secondary data, which are analysed thematically. The findings of the study show that Ankaras growing presence in the Horn of Africa offers opportunities for Ethiopia in the areas of economic development, counter-piracy, counter-terrorism and regional stability. The findings also show that Ankara has played an important role in promoting regional peace, stability and humanitarian diplomacy through its active mediation and conflict resolution to defuse conflicts and create an environment conducive to stability. Despite its significant contributions to the Horn of Africa, Turkeys growing presence in the region does not mean that the region is completely safe from competition. Turkeys growing presence in the Horn of Africa faces significant challenges due to the competing interests of Middle Eastern countries, particularly the United Arab Emirates, Israel, Saudi Arabia and Iran. These competing alliances have the potential to complicate Ethiopias security environment and undermine joint efforts for peace and development in the region. Therefore, Ethiopia needs a rational and assertive foreign policy and collective security to mitigate the risks of competition with rival Middle Eastern powers, which is essential for lasting peace and stability in the region.
Title: Turkeys strategic engagement in the Horn of Africa and its implications for Ethiopias security

Abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into research, teaching, and learning within Ghanaian universities remains underexplored, particularly with regard to context-specific ethical considerations. This study addresses this gap by investigating the relevance of GenAI in doctoral-level academia, the ethical challenges it poses, and potential strategies for its responsible implementation. Employing a qualitative, exploratory case study design grounded in normative ethics theory, the research involved semi-structured phone interviews with 12 participants, six academic instructors and six PhD candidates from the University of Ghana, selected through purposive judgmental sampling. The research followed rigorous ethical protocols. Findings indicate that GenAI can significantly enhance academic productivity by improving research quality, facilitating literature reviews, streamlining data analysis, supporting teaching preparation, and enabling personalized learning experiences. Nonetheless, participants identified several ethical concerns, including threats to academic integrity, data privacy issues, algorithmic bias, a lack of clear institutional and national AI policies. To address these issues, participants recommended measures such as training for staff and students on ethical AI use and the development of comprehensive institutional guidelines. This study contributes to the growing discourse on GenAI ethics in higher education in Ghana, highlighting the need for tailored, context-aware approaches to ensure its ethical and effective integration.
Title: Exploring the role and ethical concerns of generative AI in doctoral education at the University of Ghana

Abstract: This study examines changes in land use and land cover (LULC) in the peri-urban interface of Agra city, India. The rapid and often unregulated urban expansion in such transitional zones raises critical concerns for sustainable land management. Despite this, limited studies have focused on the long-term LULC dynamics and their driving forces in medium-sized Indian cities. Addressing this gap, the present study employs remote sensing and GIS techniques to analyze LULC changes over a 40-year period from 1981 to 2021. For identifying the land use land cover changes study utilizes Landsat-3 Multispectral Scanner (1981), Landsat-5 Thematic Mapper (2001), and Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager and Thermal Infra-Red Sensor (2021) imagery. Supervised classification technique was employed to categories for delineating land use and land cover types. Present study assessed the classification accuracy utilizing the kappa coefficient and total accuracy metrics. The results reveal a significant expansion in built-up areas by 382.13%, increasing from 20.87 sq. km in 1981 to 100.62 sq. km in 2021, indicating intensive urban growth in the peri-urban zone. Wasteland expanded by 16.50%, from 129.97 sq. km to 151.41 sq. km during 1981 to 2021. In contrast, agricultural land declined sharply by -25.84%, falling from 208.13 sq. km to 154.35 sq. km during 1981 to 2021. Forest covers and water bodies decreased by -61.08% and 12.25% respectively. The highest rate of LULC change occurred between 2001 and 2021, corresponding with intensified population growth and infrastructure development. These transformations are primarily driven by population growth, urban development, and socio-economic shifts. The findings of this study offer insights on alterations in land use and land cover and their driving forces, which Agra district authorities can utilize to formulate sustainable development strategies. While the study provides valuable insights, it is not without limitations. Factors such as classification errors, moderate spatial resolution of satellite imagery, and seasonal variability may have introduced some uncertainty in the analysis.
Title: Spatio-temporal analysis of land use and land cover dynamics in the peri-urban interface of Agra city, India

Abstract: Data drives our world today, and content generation is a very rewarding task. Traditionally content in any form (text, audio, images, etc.) are human generated, and often require experienced individuals for its inception. Large Language Models are processing units that are capable of generating content based on some large corpus of pre-fed data.ChatGPTis one of the popular text based Large Language Model. Now, since machines are capable of replicating human actions, competition evidently draws in and lately, such man-machine qualitative contrast gained a lot of attention. This research is towards the same directions, but is more of an evidence based, quantitative approach towards the comparison. To test both the subjects (machine and human intelligence), in this research we use CSES Problem Set (CSESPS), a collective set of problems that requires devising algorithms to solve them. Though, CSESPS contains several problems categories, we tend to check the programming skills, logic building, and geometric interpretation abilities of our subjects. Thus, for the analysis we considered problems from three specific categories, Introductory Problems, Mathematics, and Geometry. The statistical / empirical analysis conducted through our research evidences the lagging capabilities of machine intelligence than human intelligence. Quantitively, we conclude that Machines (to this day) are 46% less abled then average Human Intelligence (averaged for humans across the globe).
Title: An evidence-based quantitative judgment of artificial intelligence on exact sciences

Abstract: Marriage has a crucial role in the establishment of families. In this review paper, a comprehensive bibliometric examination of forced marriage, child marriage, and contract marriage is offered. It provides a profound understanding of the data that has been published, as well as recent breakthroughs, research trends, and important issues. We conducted exhaustive searches in the Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection databases between the years 2000 and 2024 by making use of the widely used RStudio software for analysis. A 19.07% yearly growth rate, the largest publication numbers (264) in 2024, PLOS ONE as the highest publisher (51 articles), author Anita Raj publishing 38 papers, Ellsberg et al. (The lancet 385:1555-1566, 2015) collecting 474 citations, and the University of London publishing the highest articles (103 respectively) are some of the data that we have uncovered. As comparable author nations (395), the United States of America came in first place, and it was also the most cited country (6969), with the term cloud child marriage ranking first, with 239 examples. The purpose of this study is to provide the framework for future research by conducting a synthesis of the global literature on forced marriage, child marriage, and contract marriage.
Title: Visualization of scopus and WOS data (20002024) on forced, child, and contract marriage: a bibliometric analysis

Abstract: Women domestic workers all over the world are a group that needs to be addressed and problematized. This becomes particularly imperative in Iran, where there is a glaring absence of protective laws and official recognition for this group, compounded by a lack of research on the subject. In this phenomenological study, the sample population is women aged 25 to 55 engaged in domestic work in Tehran, the largest metropolis in Iran. Tehran stands out for having the highest concentration of women in the service sector, informal jobs, and immigration. Employing feminist phenomenology, derived from the application of Merleau-Pontys existential phenomenology within a feminist framework, the research utilizes interpretive phenomenological analysis as its method of data analysis. The research identifies three major themes: the concepts of the available body, fusion, and possibilities of transition (identity). The findings emphasize that the challenges these women face are not isolated incidents but are deeply rooted in long-term structural and policy components, exacerbating social inequalities within paid domestic work. It has caused a devalued, vulnerable and full of discriminatory micro-scale mechanisms, highlighting the need for comprehensive efforts to address these issues. Finally, this study has tried to show unfamiliar areas of agency and identity rethinking in private space.
Title: Woman domestic worker as a situated body: a feminist phenomenology on women domestic workers in Tehran

Abstract: Aiming to contribute to international research on innovative teaching methods, this study investigates the effectiveness of the debate-driven negotiation cycle strategy (DDNCS) in enhancing self-efficacy among sixth-grade students. A quasi-experimental design was employed that involved 68 students from two schools in Muscat, Oman. The students were divided into an experimental group (34 students) who were taught a Forces and Motion unit using the DDNCS, and a control group (34 students) who were taught through traditional instruction. Pre- and post-tests using validated General and Academic Self-Efficacy Scales were used to measure the impact of the intervention. Results showed no statistically significant differences in General Self-Efficacy between the two groups, which aligns with expectations given the short intervention period and the stable nature of this construct. However, a statistically significant improvement in Academic Self-Efficacy was observed among the experimental group. Although the effect size was modest ( = 0.08), there was a meaningful impact from the debate-based strategy on students academic confidence and engagement. These findings suggest that integrating structured scientific debate into science education may enhance academic self-efficacy and, as a result, support learner motivation and active participation. However, the generalizability of the results is limited by the small sample size and unique cultural context. This study provides a foundation for further research and cautious exploration of debate-driven strategies in science pedagogy and educational policy.
Title: Exploring differences in early academic self-efficacy: the role of debate-driven negotiation in science learning for young learners

Abstract: This paper introduces a visual methodology, photo elicitation (PE), to study farming resilience in the context of transnational private governance. It focuses on seven Participatory Guarantee Systems (PGS) farms within the Thungthong Yangyeun Producer Group in Thailand. Considerable research has looked at the resilience of farming systems focusing on the crucial aspects of adaptation, transformation, and robustness. Nevertheless, our understanding of how farming resilience can be cultivated in PGS farms remains limited, while visual methods have rarely been used to study the resilience of farming practices, especially in the field of International Relations. In addition, exploring spirituality, values, and the relationships between humans and non-humans is crucial for understanding farming resilience, yet it remains a challenging endeavour thus far. The findings indicate that PE effectively addresses these gaps by sparking engaging and meaningful group discussions, encouraging introspection, and establishing links to individual and collective memories and past experiences. Photos serve as a bridge between researchers and farmers, enabling access to complex data. The paper concludes that analysing farming resilience using PE offers fresh insights into how PGS farmers enhance adaptability, transformability, and robustness amidst crises. It reveals how spirituality and human-nonhuman relationships play crucial roles in transnational private governance. The innovative visual data collection tools, verbal and non-verbal communication techniques, and the methods for data analysis developed in this research can be applied in future studies within the field of International Relations and across a range of social science disciplines.
Title: Unearthing farming resilience: insights from photo elicitation

Abstract: This case study examines government preschool teachers perceptions and practices of play-based pedagogy (PBP) in Hawassa City, Ethiopia, within Ethiopias ECCE policy promoting child-centered, developmentally appropriate learning. Despite policy endorsements, classroom practices frequently prioritize traditional, teacher-centered approaches. Grounded in Vygotskys Sociocultural Theory, Piagets Cognitive-Developmental Theory, and Bronfenbrenners Ecological Systems Theory, the study explores the alignment between teachers perceptions and practices. Data from classroom observations, semi-structured interviews with 12 teachers across four preschools, and document analysis reveal a policy-practice gap. Teachers value play but face barriers including large class sizes, limited resources, insufficient training, and parental pressure for academic outcomes. The study recommends targeted interventions, such as refined policy guidelines, ongoing professional development, and improved resource allocation, to enhance play-based pedagogy integration in Ethiopias early childhood education system.
Title: Teachers perceptions and practices of play-based pedagogy in Ethiopia preschools

Abstract: The paper examined whether violent extremism currently widespread in Nigerias sociopolitical space has been exacerbated by the sole use of military approach to address the security threats. Incessant fatal attacks, raging across almost all the geopolitical zones, have wantonly truncated economic development and peaceful coexistence. Literally, it exposed the poor administration of the security institutions that seem to have maintained a corrupt stance that led to the persistence and growth of terrorism. In this context, there is palpable fear that the spate of violence would, ultimately, push the country into a failed-state status. Consequently, the paper argued that the sole application of military option has been found wanting and requires viable alternatives. The failed/fragile state theory logically explained the tenets of the study while embracing the qualitative  descriptive method of data collection. Findings revealed that the sole kinetic option to combat violence has truncated the timely stoppage of insurgent terrorist groups and diehard criminals. Suggestively, the leaders of all militant groups should be summoned by the government for peaceful negotiations. Again, seeking foreign assistance is advocated and predicated upon embracing an e-counterinsurgency strategy, which is embedded in Artificial Intelligence technology to complement the existing military method.
Title: Perennial insecurity challenges and Nigerias military approach to eradicating extreme violence: evoking an e-counterinsurgency strategy

Abstract: Sri Lankas bankruptcy declaration on July 6, 2022, exposed deep structural weaknesses in its economic governance and external debt management. Dominant narratives often attribute the crisis to a Chinese debt trap; however, this study challenges these claims through a multi-perspective analysis using the WhyWhat framework. The findings reveal that Sri Lankas economic collapse was not driven solely by Chinese financing or the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) but rather by a combination of domestic policy failuresfor instance, unsustainable tax cuts, flawed agricultural reforms, and excessive external borrowingalongside external shocks, including the COVID-19 pandemic and the RussiaUkraine war. In contrast to geopolitical narratives, empirical evidence demonstrates that Sri Lankas debt burden is distributed among multiple creditors, including multilateral institutions and other bilateral lenders. This study contributes to the discourse on sovereign debt by reframing Sri Lankas crisis as an outcome of governance and policy failures rather than a result of external debt entrapment. Based on these findings, key policy recommendations include strengthening fiscal and monetary stability, restructuring and diversifying debt obligations, promoting economic diversification, enhancing governance and institutional transparency, and establishing expert-driven economic policymaking. These measures are crucial for rebuilding investor confidence, enhancing economic resilience, and fostering sustainable growth. This study highlights the importance of sound fiscal policies, diversified economic strategies, and transparent governance in mitigating financial vulnerabilities in an increasingly interconnected global financial system. This study argues that the debt-trap diplomacy narrative oversimplifies Sri Lankas crisis and calls for a more evidence-based, structural analysis.
Title: Sri Lankas economic crisis: facts and fiction

Abstract: Higher education institutions are embedded within distinct cultural and pedagogical contexts that shape teaching, learning, and intercultural engagement. This study examines the academic experiences of exchange students participating in international programs at Hochschule Dsseldorf University of Applied Sciences (HSD) in Germany and the University for Development Studies (UDS) in Ghana. Employing a qualitative methodology, the research utilized in-depth interviews and participant observations to explore how students navigate and adapt to the contrasting institutional and cultural dynamics of these universities. The findings highlight the complexities of intercultural communication and pedagogical adaptation, revealing the challenges and opportunities inherent in cross-cultural academic environments. Key themes include the significance of cultural awareness, institutional inclusivity, and adaptive learning strategies in fostering equitable educational experiences. The study offers practical recommendations for policy and practice to enhance the integration and support of diverse student populations in international exchange programs.
Title: University culture, communication, learning and pedagogy in international student exchange programme

Abstract: This study examines student engagement in maritime simulator-based training. It explores how maritime instructors perceive and utilise full-mission bridge simulator-based training to engage undergraduate students in learning the profession. Online semi-structured interviews are conducted with nautical simulator instructors (n=10) in four Norwegian bachelors degree programmes. The study analyses the data thematically, based on sociocultural perspectives on learning as an analytical lens. The findings are categorised into two main themes describing simulator-based training as (1) an active and participatory learning environment and (2) engagement connected to the profession. The results show instructors view simulator-based training as enabling active and participatory activities that engage students through embodied participation in domain-specific tasks, guided by the expert maritime instructors. Engagement is enhanced when students can visualise their future working environment by practising real-world-based activities, such as incidents and accidents, using maritime-specific equipment, and performing assigned professional roles. By expanding the understanding of engagement from a sociocultural perspective, this study contributes to the development of simulator-based training and instruction in maritime education.
Title: Engaging in simulations: analysing maritime instructors perceptions of student engagement

Abstract: Although online learning has become an essential component of higher education, especially in the wake of global disruptions like the COVID-19 pandemic, limited research has examined how students perceive its economic benefits and costs, particularly through the lens of demographic variables such as gender and employment status. Grounded in Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT), this study investigates students perceptions of the economic implications of online learning at the University of Ghana, specifically focusing on differences across gender and employment groups. EVT suggests that students engagement and evaluation of academic experiences are shaped by the perceived value and associated costs of those experiences. Using a quantitative research design, survey data were collected from 338 students via Google Forms distributed through student WhatsApp groups with the consent of group administrators. The data were analyzed using SPSS, employing descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and analysis of variance. Findings indicate that while online learning is broadly perceived as economically beneficial, especially among employed students, it also entails significant financial burdens related to internet access, digital devices, and electricity. These burdens disproportionately affect unemployed students, limiting equitable access to online learning opportunities. Gender-based differences were also observed, with male students reporting marginally greater economic benefits than females. The study contributes to the limited empirical literature on the economic dimensions of online learning in developing contexts, offering insights for policymakers to design more inclusive and equitable digital education frameworks. Recommendations are made for future research, including longitudinal studies, cross-cultural analyses, and examining emerging technologies in shaping students economic experiences with online education.
Title: Perceived economic benefits and costs of online learning: the role of gender and employment status among students at the University of Ghana

Abstract: The cleaning industry plays a crucial role in maintaining hygiene, yet the experiences of its workers, particularly with technological advancements in the workplace, are underexplored. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the adoption of advanced sanitation technologies, including advanced cleaning robots, making it essential to understand how cleaning workers adapt to these changes. As a result, this study examined the lived experiences of nine cleaning workers, primarily from lower-income backgrounds and immigrant families throughout the Caribbean region, using a phenomenological approach. The research highlights the unique challenges these workers face, including limited formal education and the need to adapt to new technologies. Work Adjustment Theory (WAT) was applied to understand the processes of adaptation and the impact of socioeconomic factors on job satisfaction and efficiency. The findings reveal that while technology integration improves job quality and reduces physical strain, there are significant gaps in training that need to be addressed. The study emphasizes the importance of tailored training programs and explores the positive relationship between technology and job satisfaction. It also discusses the theoretical implications of WAT in the context of low-income workers adaptation to technological changes. This research contributes to the understanding of technologys intersection with the cleaning industry and its impact on worker well-being and organizational practices.
Title: A phenomenological exploration of cleaning industry workers experiences in the era of technical advancements

Abstract: Countries in the global south, such as Ghana, can harness the transformative potential of the digital age by integrating effective computer-based learning into their educational system. This study examined the extent to which Junior High Schools (JHS) in Ghana are responding to emerging computer-based learning approaches, with particular emphasis on students awareness and application of digital technologies. Employing a mixed-method design, the research concurrently collected qualitative and quantitative data from students, teachers, headmasters, and school administrators. The sample comprised 214 JHS students from Kumasi Metropolis, Ghana, complemented by in-depth interviews with 8 key stakeholders, including teachers, headmasters, and school administrators. Findings revealed limited policy focus and a relatively low level of student awareness regarding emerging computer-based learning approaches. The study recommends revising the national ICT in Education Policy to incorporate contemporary digital skills, such as coding, robotics, and tablet-based learning, at the basic education level. More importantly, it underscores the need for targeted policy interventions to ensure adequate technological infrastructure and skilled human resources to advance computer-based learning in Ghanas JHS.
Title: Ghanas educational system in the digital age: an assessment of the responsiveness of Junior High School education to computer-based learning

Abstract: The objective of this study is to explore the mediating effect of learning engagement on the relationship between learning self-efficacy, learner interaction, emotion regulation, and perceived learning among Chinese secondary school students in an online mathematics learning environment. This research adopted a quantitative approach with a predictive correlational design, involving 605 participants selected through simple random sampling. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) was employed to analyse the collected data. The SEM analysis revealed a significant positive relationship between learning self-efficacy, learner interaction, emotion regulation, and perceived learning. Bootstrapping results indicated that learning engagement partially mediates the relationships between learning self-efficacy and perceived learning, learner interaction and perceived learning, as well as emotion regulation and perceived learning. These findings enhance our understanding of the critical roles that learning self-efficacy, learner interaction, emotion regulation, and perceived learning play, with learning engagement acting as a mediator in the context of online mathematics learning.
Title: The role of learning engagement in shaping the relationship between self-efficacy, interaction, emotion regulation and perceived learning in online education

Abstract: The Italian National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), launched in January 2021, channels EU funds from the Next Generation EU program to support Italys post-Covid recovery. From the outset, its implementation has encountered major challenges due to the administrative and organizational demands on recipient entities, many of which lack sufficient expertise. To help, philanthropic organizations have provided training, capacity-building, and tailored support. However, new issuesespecially delays in publishing funding callshave created a widespread impasse, threatening to undermine such efforts. This study explores whether these delays stem from insufficient skills among staff or other causes. Using data from the Next Generation WE project, led by the Compagnia di San Paolo Foundation, we analysed 148 organizations from Northwestern Italy. About 40%mostly those in final projecting phaseswere still awaiting funding calls. We examined this 40%, focusing on two factors: project complexity (technological and managerial) and staff participation in training. A rigorously trained generative AI, using the SMART-E framework, scored each proposal on these dimensions. Results were statistically compared using point biserial correlation. Findings partially support the initial hypothesis: there is a slight inverse correlation between staff training and stalled funding calls. However, neither technological complexity nor managerial difficulty consistently predicts which projects remain unfunded. Thus, the root causes of the delays likely lie beyond the technical or organizational characteristics of the projects themselves.
Title: Private philantropy supporting the implementation of next generation EU in Italy: a generative artificial intelligence study

Abstract: Affective polarization, marked by deep emotional divides among political groups, has become a pressing global concern with far-reaching social and political consequences. This study presents the first bibliometric analysis of scholarly research on affective polarization in Asia, providing a systematic and contextualized overview of academic trends, knowledge production, and thematic developments in the region. In line with the PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a comprehensive review using SCOPUS and Web of Science databases, and analysed 80 key articles published from 1989 to 2023. Bibliometric analysis was performed using Biblioshiny within R Studio. The findings reveal a marked increase in research over the past decade, particularly between 2018 and 2023, reflecting heightened scholarly interest in affective polarization across Asian contexts. China and South Korea emerged as leading contributors, while countries such as India and regions like Central Asia remain underrepresented. Communication studies dominated in publication output, underscoring the critical role of media and digital platforms in influencing political attitudes. Thematic mapping showed a dynamic research landscape increasingly focused on the interplay between affective polarization, social media use, political communication, and social fragmentation.
